Article Title: In 1926, a 10-foot rocket rose just 41 feet from a Massachusetts farm; 35 years later, NASA put its creator’s name in space
Article Text:
A replica of the world's first liquid propellant rocket, PC: Wikimedia Commons

Why Robert Goddard's 1926 rocket mattered more than its brief flight suggested

How Goddard's early work went largely unrecognised during his lifetime

Why NASA chose Goddard's name for its new spaceflight centre

On March 16, 1926, on a snowy farm in Auburn, Massachusetts, physicist Robert H. Goddard set up a slim, 10-foot rocket he had nicknamed Nell on a launch frame in an open field. Fueled by gasoline and liquid oxygen, the rocket climbed just 41 feet into the air, flew for only 2.5 seconds, and crashed back to Earth 184 feet from where it started. The witnesses were Goddard, his wife Esther, crew chief Henry Sachs and Clark University physics professor Percy Roope. The flight attracted little attention at the time, and Goddard kept the achievement largely private for years. Yet that brief flight marked the world's first successful launch of a liquid-fueled rocket, demonstrating that a rocket could be powered by liquid propellants rather than relying solely on solid fuel. The breakthrough became a foundation for modern rocketry and, decades later, helped earn Goddard a place in the history of human spaceflight. Thirty-five years later, NASA formally honoured him by dedicating its Goddard Space Flight Centre in his name.According to NASA's history office , Goddard had experimented with solid-fuel rockets years earlier, including work dating to the World War I era. He began experimenting with liquid-fueled rocket engines in September 1921, eventually developing the technology that led to his historic 1926 launch. By December 1925, he had successfully tested a liquid-fueled engine independently of its launch frame, setting the stage for the flight that followed a few months later.What made the 1926 experiment significant was not its altitude but what it demonstrated: liquid propellants could be controlled and burned to produce rocket thrust. Goddard's work also rested on patents he had secured in 1914, including designs for a rocket combustion chamber and nozzle and a multistage rocket capable of reaching high altitudes. The National Park Service, which oversees the Goddard Rocket Launching Site as a National Historic Landmark, recognises these early developments as important milestones in the history of modern rocketry.Despite the importance of his experiments, Goddard received little public or scientific support during much of his career, and some of his theories were openly ridiculed. His situation improved after he received financial backing from the Guggenheim Fund for the Promotion of Aeronautics, with support from aviator Charles Lindbergh. That funding allowed him to establish a dedicated testing site in Roswell, New Mexico, where he conducted rocket experiments from 1930 to 1942.Goddard achieved 31 successful rocket flights at the Roswell site, including one that reached an altitude of 1.7 miles in 22.3 seconds. His rockets incorporated increasingly sophisticated technologies, including gyroscopic stabilisation and turbopumps designed to feed propellants into the combustion chamber. Yet much of his work remained relatively obscure in the United States while Germany pursued rocket development on a much larger scale. German engineers eventually developed the V-2, the world's first long-range guided ballistic missile, which was used against Britain and other European targets during World War II. Goddard died in 1945, before the major advances in rocketry of the 1950s and 1960s. He therefore never saw the emergence of the space programs that would ultimately use many of the principles he had spent decades developing.NASA established the Goddard Space Flight Centre in Greenbelt, Maryland, in 1959, naming it after the pioneering rocket scientist whose work had helped establish the foundations of liquid-fueled rocketry. The facility was formally dedicated on March 16, 1961, exactly 35 years after Goddard's historic first liquid-fueled rocket launch. The original launch site in Auburn, Massachusetts, is now recognised as a National Historic Landmark by the National Park Service. A granite marker commemorates the location where Goddard conducted the experiment, which lasted only seconds and produced a flight measured in feet rather than miles.At the time, there was little indication that the small rocket launched from a Massachusetts farm would have such a lasting legacy. But Goddard had demonstrated something fundamental: liquid-fueled rockets could work. Decades later, the same basic principle would underpin the rockets used to launch satellites, send astronauts into orbit and carry humans to the Moon.
Article Summary: Goddard's 1926 launch was the world's first successful launch of a liquid-fueled rocket. The rocket climbed just 41 feet into the air, flew for only 2.5 seconds, and crashed back to Earth 184 feet from where it started. Thirty-five years later, NASA formally honoured him by dedicating its Goddard Space Flight Centre in his name.

Article Title: US wildfire crisis: Hawk Fire burns more than 15,000 acres, forcing mass evacuations in Nevada
Article Text:
In Nevada, 23,000 people remained under evacuation orders around Reno on Monday as the Hawk Fire burned more than 15,000 acres. (GIF: @HotshotWake)

Families flee as Hawk Fire reaches Reno homes

Fire threat eases, but 23,000 remain displaced

California weighs liability for utility-linked wildfires

Some western forests may never return

Scientists test ways to help forests recover

In Nevada, 23,000 people remained under evacuation orders around Reno on Monday as the Hawk Fire burned more than 15,000 acres, while California lawmakers weighed utility wildfire liability and scientists warned that up to 40% of western conifer forests could turn to shrubland by 2100.Another 40,000 residents had been told to be ready to leave around Reno, while at least 32 homes had been destroyed. The number of residents either displaced or preparing to flee had fallen to about 63,000 from an estimated 90,000 over the weekend.Firefighters had contained 27% of the blaze, while six more homes were damaged. Four civilians and three emergency personnel suffered minor burns, but no deaths have been reported.Evacuation notices covered parts of northwest Reno between the Sierra Nevada foothills and the University of Nevada. Television footage showed fire nearing roads, while verified eyewitness video captured smoke spreading from the hills over residential areas, according to news agency Reuters.For some families, evacuation meant taking whatever they could before the fire arrived. Luke Opperman, 47, was camping when flames reached the Reno neighbourhood where his family had lived for nearly 20 years.His wife and two teenage daughters loaded clothes and important possessions into three cars and two trailers. They also took the family’s chickens, goats, dog and cats.Their home was destroyed along with six neighbouring houses. Opperman estimated that as many as 20 homes had burned in his immediate community adjoining the Humboldt-Toiyabe National Forest.“It’s more than just a house; it’s your neighborhood, it’s your community,” he said. The uncertainty did not end with the evacuation, with Opperman adding: “I think it’s baby steps. I don’t know what’s happening at the end of this week.”Firefighters had contained 27% of the Hawk Fire by Monday, while officials said the blaze had stopped expanding and remained at roughly 23 square miles.Authorities had reduced the number of people covered by evacuation orders or warnings to about 63,000. Of them, 23,000 remained under “go-now” orders and another 40,000 were told to stay ready to leave at short notice.Easing winds gave crews some relief, though heat and low humidity continued to complicate firefighting. Officials remained wary of fresh gusts carrying the fire across dry vegetation towards residential development.At least 32 homes had been destroyed and six damaged. Officials said the property toll was expected to rise as assessment teams surveyed more of the burned area.Evacuations also closed Washoe County schools on Monday, helping keep roads clear for emergency crews. Some residents complained after being prevented from returning home, but Sheriff Darin Balaam said the danger had not passed and warned about the risk posed by even a light breeze and a single ember, according to news agency Associated Press.More than 900 firefighters were working on the Hawk Fire by Monday. Crews came from 15 US states, while firefighters from Australia and New Zealand were also deployed as international teams helped tackle blazes across the western US.Nevada governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency in Washoe County. Lombardo authorised two National Guard helicopters to help fight the fire and 60 Guard personnel to support the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office.Officials said the fire was human-caused, though investigators had not determined whether it was started deliberately or accidentally. It follows another major fire in the Truckee River valley in recent weeks.The evacuation perimeter did not reach Reno-Tahoe International Airport, where commercial flights continued normally on Sunday.The destruction around Reno raises another question that California has been confronting for years: who bears the financial burden when utility equipment starts a wildfire? California law makes utilities responsible for damage from fires caused by their equipment even if a court does not find them negligent. Insurers that pay homeowners for rebuilding can later seek reimbursement from the utility involved.California governor Gavin Newsom is trying to change how those costs are divided.His proposal could reduce the financial exposure of electricity and gas companies, get money to survivors sooner and shift a greater share of property losses to insurers, according to news agency Associated Press. Newsom says another goal is to stabilize electricity prices, with California’s power rates among the highest in the country and continuing to rise as utilities spend more on wildfire prevention and recovery.A $21 billion wildfire fund created under legislation Newsom signed in 2019 is part of the existing system. Utility shareholders and ratepayers finance the fund, which helps companies meet wildfire liabilities if they fulfil specified safety requirements, but Newsom says the fund could soon run out.A Northern California fire that began two days after Newsom won the governorship in 2018 killed 85 people and destroyed more than 18,000 buildings. Investigators traced the fire to Pacific Gas & Electric equipment, and the utility later filed for bankruptcy while facing tens of billions of dollars in liabilities.Another fire outside Los Angeles in 2025 killed 19 people and became the state’s second-most destructive wildfire. Investigators this month found that a Southern California Edison transmission tower started the blaze, while utility equipment has caused six of California’s 10 most destructive wildfires.Under Newsom’s proposal, insurers could have to cover a larger share of property losses, while limits could be placed on what utilities pay victims and attorneys. Utility executives could lose bonuses if their company’s equipment causes more than $1 billion in wildfire damage, while shareholders could also face penalties of up to $10 million for violating wildfire-prevention requirements.The governor’s office has not yet released the proposal in full. Fire survivors and property insurers have opposed parts of the plan, arguing that it would shift too much responsibility away from utilities.California Professional Firefighters has backed the proposal, saying financial stability must be balanced with the ability of affected communities to recover and rebuild. Lawmakers have until August 31 to act, while Newsom could call a special session if no agreement is reached. The Legislature also approved another $18 billion last year after Newsom proposed supplementing the wildfire fund. The latest debate comes as California continues to grapple with the financial consequences of increasingly destructive wildfires.The immediate question for Reno’s evacuees is whether they will have homes to return to. Scientists across the West are confronting a longer-term concern: some forests destroyed by increasingly severe fires may not return at all. Recent studies estimate that as much as 40% of conifer forests in the western US could turn into shrubland by 2100 as hotter fires and a warmer climate interfere with natural regeneration, according to The New York Times.In some western states, snowmelt accounts for as much as three-quarters of the water supply. Without tree cover, snow can melt earlier, while hotter and drier conditions can also remove moisture from soil and vegetation. That can leave plants more vulnerable to fire. Mature forests also store substantial amounts of carbon. Large, older trees hold more carbon than younger trees and shrubs, meaning the conversion of forest into lower vegetation reduces that storage capacity.Wildfires have turned roughly 1,700 acres once covered by centuries-old ponderosa pines into shrubland. Scientists say the forest is unlikely to return. Researchers examining land burned by the 2022 Oak Fire found no new ponderosa pine seedlings. Under more typical conditions, young trees emerge after a fire and can rebuild a forest over one or two decades.About one-fifth of conifers across the Sierra Nevada are already poorly suited to the region’s warmer climate. Forest ecologist Winslow Hansen remembers a different kind of recovery after his family evacuated their home near Bozeman, Montana, during a wildfire in 2000, when he was 13.Firefighters saved the house, and young tree seedlings appeared in the burned forest the following year. Some fire-damaged forests today are responding differently, with natural regeneration failing altogether.Researchers found a more favourable outcome at land burned by California’s 2013 Rim Fire. Ponderosa pines survived there and new trees are growing among shrubs. The Rim Fire site and the Oak Fire site receive similar rainfall and sit at about the same elevation, but their soils differ sharply. Testing found fungus levels at the Rim site were about 6.5 times higher, bacteria levels about four times higher and organic matter about 1.5 times greater. The Rim Fire soil also had high levels of nitrogen and phosphorus, both important for plant growth. The risk of failed regeneration is particularly severe in the drier Southwest.Northern New Mexico’s Jemez Mountains have burned twice since the 1970s, leaving much of the former forest nearly without trees. Researchers also examined nearly 3,500 wildfires that burned conifer forests in Canada and the western US between 2012 and 2023.Their study found that some fires are becoming so large and spreading so quickly that pine seeds can no longer successfully regenerate forests. The findings add to concerns that repeated fires may permanently alter some western landscapes.In Montana, scientists moved western larch seedlings from warmer, lower elevations into higher areas damaged by fire. Those seedlings performed better in warmer conditions than seedlings taken from higher elevations.Researchers in California and Washington are conducting similar assisted-migration experiments, using plants from warmer conditions to help burned forests recover. Scientists say predicting which forests will survive remains difficult despite advances in remote sensing, genetic analysis and climate modelling.Temperature, moisture and soil conditions can point towards an outcome, but researchers say the biological response remains uncertain. That uncertainty continues to complicate efforts to determine where forests can recover naturally and where intervention may be needed.
Article Summary: Firefighters had contained 27% of the Hawk Fire by Monday, while officials said the blaze had stopped expanding. Another 40,000 residents had been told to be ready to leave around Reno, while at least 32 homes had been destroyed. Four civilians and three emergency personnel suffered minor burns, but no deaths were reported.

Article Title: Pakistan army officer pulls gun, fires in air amid student protest at Peshawar university- video
Article Text:
Sarhad University, Peshawar, Pakistan (Picture from X)

A Pakistan army officer opened fire into the air during a student protest at Sarhad University in Peshawar, triggering chaos and a scuffle on the campus, according to local media reports and videos circulating online.The incident comes amid growing unrest in Pakistan, with protests and demonstrations also being reported from Pakistan-occupied Kashmir and Balochistan, adding to the challenges facing the country's military and political establishment.According to reports, the officer, said to be a colonel, was the husband of a faculty member at Sarhad University. He reportedly got into a heated confrontation with protesting students, which soon escalated into a physical scuffle.Videos shared by several social media accounts purportedly show the officer striking students with a stick amid the confrontation. As tensions escalated, he allegedly pulled out a pistol and initially pointed it towards the protesters before raising the weapon in the air.The officer was then seen firing shots into the air, sparking panic and further uproar on the university campus.Reports said the officer has been taken into custody, while the Pakistan army has ordered an inquiry into the incident.
Article Summary: Pakistan army officer opened fire during student protest at Sarhad University. Incident triggered chaos and a scuffle on the campus, according to reports. Incident comes amid growing unrest in Pakistan, with protests and demonstrations also being reported from Pakistan-occupied Kashmir and Balochistan.

Article Title: ‘Must correct its tone’: Iran’s Pezeshkian warns US against ‘coercion and bullying’ in Munir meet
Article Text:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, right, meets Pakistan's Army chief Asim Munir in Tehran, Iran (Picture credit: AP)

Pezeshkian stresses regional cooperation, unity

Munir’s Iran visit follows Trump call

Iran faces fresh US economic pressure

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has told Pakistan Army chief Asim Munir that the United States must change its approach towards Tehran, warning that “coercion and bullying” would complicate diplomatic efforts.Pezeshkian made the remarks during a meeting with Munir in Tehran on Monday, according to the official website of the Iranian President.Munir arrived in Iran for talks with Iranian officials amid heightened regional tensions and continuing friction between Tehran and Washington.The Iranian president also expressed hope that continued cooperation between Iran and Pakistan would help achieve the goals outlined in a 14-point Memorandum of Understanding (MoU).“The United States must correct its tone and approach in its interactions with Iran, because relying on coercion and bullying will only complicate the implementation processes,” Pezeshkian said.He stressed that Washington should adhere to its commitments to Iran based on international law and standards.Pezeshkian also said Iran would withstand pressure by relying on national solidarity.“Our nation will overcome any pressure and threat by relying on this solidarity,” he said.During the meeting, Pezeshkian stressed the need for lasting peace and security in the region and called for greater cooperation with Islamic countries and neighbouring states.“The Islamic Republic of Iran is ready for any cooperation and interaction in the economic, political, and security dimensions with Islamic countries and neighbours, because the Holy Prophet (PBUH) has always commanded peace and friendship,” he said.He also emphasised the importance of unity among Islamic countries, describing it as a deterrent against what he called the “conspiracies of the Zionist regime and the enemies of Islam”.“The unity and cohesion of Islamic countries is the most important deterrent against the conspiracies of the Zionist regime and the enemies of Islam, and if this convergence is realised, the enemies will not be able to advance their sinister goals,” Pezeshkian said.The Iranian president also referred to coordination within Iran to advance regional peace and stability and expressed hope that Pakistan's diplomatic efforts would contribute to stability in the region.He said he hoped the “Islamic world will achieve increasing growth, dignity, and pride”.Munir, in turn, thanked Pezeshkian for his efforts towards establishing regional stability and peace.“In order to advance common goals and achieve a comprehensive agreement, it is essential that diplomatic processes be discussed and examined with complete precision and meticulousness,” Munir said, according to the Iranian president's official website.The Pakistan Army chief also welcomed the growing trend of bilateral cooperation between the two countries.He said the “deep historical, religious and cultural commonalities between Pakistan and Iran are a valuable asset for overcoming the current complex circumstances and charting a bright future”.Munir's visit to Tehran comes after he spoke by phone with US President Donald Trump last week, according to US media reports. A source familiar with the conversation told CNN that Trump and Munir discussed Iran.Munir also met Iranian officials during his visit. Iran's state broadcaster IRIB reported that he held talks with Major General Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council.Rezaei also called on Washington to change its behaviour and take practical steps to implement the 14-point MoU.Earlier on Monday, Iranian Parliamentary Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf also met Munir in Tehran. According to a statement shared by Ghalibaf on Telegram, the two discussed what Iran described as repeated US breaches of commitments under the MoU.“The commitments of the parties in the Memorandum of Understanding are clear, and it was America that, by breaching its commitments, prevented the establishment of stability in the region and created another reason for distrust in this country,” Ghalibaf said.He said Tehran remained committed to implementing the MoU and that Iran would not be affected by external pressure.“We are pursuing the implementation of the terms of the Memorandum of Understanding, and it is America that must adhere to its commitments based on the Memorandum of Understanding,” the statement quoted him as saying.Munir also said he would continue his efforts to restore stability in the region, according to the statement.Munir's visit comes as Washington has announced fresh economic sanctions against Iran.US treasury secretary Scott Bessent on Monday unveiled new measures targeting 60 individuals, entities and vessels, while stopping short of imposing the most severe penalties threatened against countries that continue trading with Iran.Iranian economy minister Ali Madanizadeh said Tehran was prepared to respond to the new sanctions.“We are fully prepared for the US sanctions,” Madanizadeh said, according to Reuters.He said Iran had its own tools to respond to what he described as an economic attack and claimed that China and Russia had not accepted the US measures.Pakistan's earlier mediation efforts between Washington and Tehran had resulted in an interim peace agreement signed in June, but the Islamabad Memorandum subsequently faltered.Against this backdrop, Munir's meetings with Iran's top political and security officials have focused on diplomatic processes, regional stability and implementation of the 14-point MoU.
Article Summary: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has told Pakistan Army chief Asim Munir that the United States must change its approach towards Tehran. He warned that “coercion and bullying” would complicate diplomatic efforts. Munir arrived in Iran for talks with Iranian officials amid heightened regional tensions and continuing friction between Tehran and Washington.

Article Title: From Gen Z wave to heat in 150 days: Nepal PM Balen faces street anger, parliament pressure and party unease
Article Text:
Nepal PM Balen Shah faces protests, Parliament heat and RSP dissent

Barely 150 days after Gen Z anger helped propel Balendra "Balen" Shah to Nepal's top job, the same restless street energy that propelled his rise seems to be pinning him down, leaving the former rapper under pressure from public protests, parliament and his own Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP).Barely two months after he took office, young protesters returned to Kathmandu's Maitighar Mandala demanding his resignation, while opposition MPs attacked his repeated absence from parliament, where he attended only five of the first 39 sittings before speaker Dol Prasad Aryal directed him to appear and answer lawmakers on Aug 26.The political honeymoon began fraying within weeks of Shah taking office on March 27, after RSP swept 182 of 275 House seats. In April, strict enforcement of customs rules on goods brought across the open India border hit people dependent on Indian markets for groceries, medicines and household essentials, triggering protests in border towns and forcing authorities to relax the move.Public anger intensified in July after 25-year-old ride-share driver Ganesh Nepali self-immolated outside the passport office in Kathmandu following a dispute over municipal action against his vehicle.His death fuelled demonstrations over municipal policing and revived criticism of drives against informal settlements and landless squatters without adequate rehabilitation.Shah also faced sustained attacks over Nepal's border dispute with India after his statement on Nepal encroaching on India's territory drew the opposition's ire.Violent communal clashes in southern Nepal along the border with India added another layer of pressure and forced Shah to address the nation after criticism over his delayed response, while in Pokhara former Gorkha servicemen continued demanding a resolution of stalled recruitment of Nepalis into Indian Army under Agnipath.The strain has spread inside RSP, where lawmakers and senior leaders questioned Shah's distance from party structures and unilateral governing style. RSP MP Jagadish Kharel sharpened the criticism from within while speaking in Parliament, saying, "Govt will not survive if only the dignity of the PM is preserved. Our dignity must also be preserved."
Article Summary: Nepal PM Balen Shah under pressure from public protests, parliament and his own Rastriya Swatantra Party. Young protesters returned to Kathmandu's Maitighar Mandala demanding his resignation. Opposition MPs attacked his repeated absence from parliament, where he attended five of the first 39 sittings.

Article Title: Ex-Pakistan PM Imran Khan returns to Adiala Jail after medical examination at Islamabad hospital
Article Text:
73-year-old cricket legend facing health issues after 3 years of imprisonment

Former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan on Friday returned to Rawalpindi's Adiala Jail shortly after undergoing a medical examination at Shifa Hospital in Islamabad.The development was confirmed to Reuters by a member of his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party.The 73-year-old cricket legend has been facing health issues after spending more than three years in prison following his tenure as prime minister.Khan was taken to Shifa Hospital days after the Supreme Court ordered a medical examination. An official from the Shehbaz Sharif-led government said Islamabad was complying with the Supreme Court's order to facilitate his medical examination.Khan's party and family had sought permission for him to remain in hospital.A three-judge Supreme Court panel had ordered authorities two days earlier to take Khan to Shifa International Hospital for a medical examination amid prolonged concerns raised by his family and personal doctors over his health and access to treatment.The court directed that a medical board, including specialists and his personal physician, Faisal Sultan, examine him.The Supreme Court's order came after former Pakistan president Arif Alvi shared Khan's vitals and raised concerns over what he described as "alarming" medical reports.In a post on X, Alvi said, "Imran Khan's medical reports are alarming. I have gone through them with several specialists, and I am writing this in plain language so every Pakistani can understand exactly what is happening."Alvi also highlighted Khan's health concerns, citing his "anxiety and stress levels", "palpitations," and "high blood pressure." He added that while sleeplessness was not mentioned in the report, Khan's medication appeared to suggest the problem.
Article Summary: Imran Khan returned to Adiala Jail after medical examination at Shifa Hospital in Islamabad. Khan, 73, has been facing health issues after spending more than three years in prison following his tenure as prime minister. A three-judge Supreme Court panel had ordered authorities two days earlier to take Khan to Shifa International Hospital for a medical examination.

Article Title: US debt crosses $40 trillion but everyone still trusts Uncle Sam. But for how long?
Article Text:
US national debt crossed $40 trillion, exceeding annual GDP, as interest payments approach $1 trillion, with economists warning of painful adjustments ahead.

TOI correspondent from Washington:

Amid The Urge To Splurge, Trump Has Proposed Hike Of 50% In Def Budget

Surprisingly, America is not mainly borrowing from China. The biggest lenders are actually Americans and American institutions – pension funds, mutual funds, banks, insurance companies, households and investment funds. Foreign governments and investors also buy what is euphemistically called “US Treasury securities”: Japan held about $1.12 trillion in June, Britain about $940 billion, China about $633 billion and India roughly $200 billion.

Yes, Uncle Sam, we’ll take your IOU.

The United States’ national debt crossed $40 trillion on Tuesday, a number so large that even breaking it up with commas can scarcely make it comprehensible. As in a 4 followed by 13 zeroes: $40,000,000,000,000!Number-crunching economists reached for various metrics to convey the scale of the crisis. The US economy produces roughly $33 trillion worth of goods and services a year. So the debt is now bigger than the entire annual economic output (GDP) of the country. Per American, that works out to roughly $118,000; for a family of four, about $472,000. Divvying it another way, the US is adding debt at a rate of roughly $90,000 every second.To put that in perspective for readers in India, the $40 trillion debt America has racked up is roughly 10 times the size of India’s entire annual economy. In other words — although debt versus GDP is not an apples-to-apples comparison — the US owes roughly ten times the value of everything India produces in a year. America’s debt mountain is therefore not merely bigger than India’s economy; it is about ten Indian economies stacked on top of one another.Economists also put the best possible spin by pointing out that the raw number itself is less important than debt relative to the size of the economy and the government’s ability to service it.Just the US debt held by its public is roughly equal to annual GDP, and the Congressional Budget Office says that, under current law, the ratio could rise to 120% of GDP by 2036 and 175% by 2056.So how did the world’s richest country get here? In the simplest terms, Washington has been spending more than it collects in taxes — year after year, administration after administration. Wars, tax cuts, the 2008 financial crisis, Covid stimulus, an ageing population and rising Social Security and Medicare costs have all added to the bill. The pandemic was particularly spectacular: debt exploded as the government tried to prevent an economic catastrophe.But the extraordinary thing is that America has continued borrowing heavily even after the emergencies have passed. Federal budget deficits are still running at levels normally associated with wars or recessions. The awkward question for Washington now is whether the borrowing eventually stops gently — or with a crash.So who is lending America $40 trillion?But why lend to a country this deeply in debt? Because US “Treasury securities” remain the world’s favourite financial equivalent of a steel safe with a very large lock. They are highly liquid, easily traded and backed by the world’s largest economy — as well as by Washington’s long-established record of paying its debts. In other words, America has been able to borrow on an extraordinary scale because the world keeps saying:For now.President Trump has repeatedly promised to reduce the national debt, including by using tariff revenue. But the arithmetic has not exactly been taking orders from the White House. Amid the irresistible American urge to splurge, Trump is proposing a $1.5 trillion military budget, roughly a 50% increase from recent levels and an unprecedented level of Pentagon spending, arguing that a stronger military is essential to national security.So America is essentially trying to lose weight while ordering a second dessert; spending like a drunken sailor on shore leave — and then promising the bartender that tariffs will somehow pay the tab.And debt is not merely about the amount borrowed. It is also about the interest bill. Interest payments are now approaching $1 trillion a year. That means an increasing share of the federal budget is going simply toward servicing yesterday’s borrowing rather than paying for today’s schools, roads, defence, healthcare or anything else Washington wants to spend money on.As the debt grows, investors could eventually demand higher interest rates to keep buying Treasury securities. That would feed through into mortgage rates, business borrowing costs and the government’s own financing costs, potentially slowing investment and economic growth. The US would then face the unpleasant menu economists have been warning about for years: higher taxes, slower spending, cuts to benefits, faster economic growth, inflation — or some combination of all of them.Washington would have to bring spending and revenues into better balance: restrain the growth of entitlement programmes, control discretionary spending, reconsider tax cuts, raise more revenue and — hardest of all — persuade voters that there is no painless option. There is no magic button marked “Pay Off $40 Trillion.”The CBO’s is essentially warning that the longer Washington waits, the more painful the eventual adjustment becomes. That is America’s peculiar fiscal paradox: the world’s richest country can afford an enormous debt — until one day the debt becomes so enormous that it starts deciding what the world’s richest country can afford. Or as one economist might put it, there is no such thing as a free lunch -- just a lunch somebody has put on the national credit card.
Article Summary: US national debt crossed $40 trillion, exceeding annual GDP, as interest payments approach $1 trillion, with economists warning of painful adjustments ahead. To put that in perspective for readers in India, the $40 trillions debt America has racked up is roughly 10 times the size of India’s entire annual economy.

Article Title: Japan installed a 1.1 MW turbine beneath the Naru Strait, using predictable tidal currents to generate clean electricity for the Goto Islands
Article Text:
Image AI generated

How Japan’s 1.1 MW AR1100 tidal turbine generates electricity underwater

Image AI generated

Japan’s tidal energy project grows from a 500 kW pilot to a 1.1 MW turbine

Why predictable tidal energy could complement solar and wind in Japan

The engineering challenges of operating a tidal turbine underwater

Between Japan’s Goto Islands, the sea is doing something that is usually associated with wind farms and solar fields. Beneath the surface of the Naru Strait, a 1.1 MW turbine is drawing energy from water moving with the tides and sending electricity back towards land through a subsea cable. No blades are turning in the sky and no panels spread across the shoreline. The machine works largely out of sight, following currents whose timing can be forecast well in advance. Installed by Proteus Marine Renewables, the AR1100 grew from an earlier 500 kW trial in the same waters. Its deployment has given Japan a megawatt-scale tidal system designed to work with the regular rise and fall of the sea rather than depending on sunshine or changing winds.The project also demonstrates the potential of tidal power in narrow channels, where fast-moving water can provide a concentrated source of renewable energy. By placing the turbine underwater, the system avoids taking up large areas of land while tapping into a resource that follows a predictable natural cycle.Unlike solar and wind power, tidal energy has one major advantage: its timing can be predicted years ahead because tides follow the gravitational pull of the Moon and Sun.That predictability could make tidal turbines useful alongside renewable sources whose output changes with weather conditions.The AR1100 is installed in the Naru Strait near Japan’s Goto Islands. Unlike a conventional wind turbine, there is no tower standing above the water and no set of panels covering land. The generating equipment works underwater, where tidal currents pass through its three-bladed rotor and turn the machinery inside the nacelle. Electricity then travels towards shore through a subsea connection. According to Proteus Marine Renewables, the turbine was deployed in February 2025, while later company information recorded that it received Japanese certification and began exporting electricity to the grid in June 2025.The arrangement is fairly straightforward in principle, although operating it beneath the sea is not. The rotor extracts energy from moving water, the drivetrain passes that mechanical power to a permanent-magnet generator, and the resulting electricity is carried to an onshore station. A yaw system turns the nacelle as the tidal flow reverses, while independently controlled blades can alter their pitch to regulate how the turbine responds to changing conditions. AR1100 is a horizontal-axis turbine mounted on a gravity-based support structure. The earlier project in the same strait provided the starting point for the larger machine.Offshore Energy reported that the earlier 500 kW AR500 pilot operated in the Naru Strait with 97% availability in 2021. That earlier machine had a rated capacity of 500 kW and recorded 97% availability during its operation, according to the material released about the project. The experience allowed engineers to see how the technology behaved in the actual marine environment rather than only in controlled testing.The next version increased the rated capacity to 1.1 MW and introduced changes to the turbine's control systems. An equipment supply and works contract with Kyuden Mirai Energy was signed in November 2022, with the Japanese project subsequently moving towards the upgraded machine. Advanced pitch and yaw systems were incorporated as part of the work. The company says those changes were intended to improve the turbine's performance and efficiency while allowing it to deal more effectively with the changing direction of the tidal flow.The most distinctive feature of tidal power is not simply that the turbines sit underwater. It is the predictability of the resource. Solar output changes with daylight and weather conditions. Wind can strengthen, weaken or stop altogether. ClickPetroleogas noted that tidal production can be estimated in advance because the cycles follow predictable natural patterns, unlike renewable generation that is more affected by weather conditions. The electricity produced at any particular moment still depends on the conditions at the site and the performance of the equipment; the underlying movement of the water is far less of a surprise.That distinction matters when renewable sources are being combined. A grid operator cannot make the sun shine or order the wind to blow, whereas the timing of tidal cycles can be incorporated into generation planning. It does not make tidal energy constant; the flow rises and falls as the tide changes, but it makes the pattern easier to anticipate. For islands such as those around the Goto group, where space and fuel logistics can present particular constraints, a submerged source can sit alongside solar, wind and other forms of generation. The Naru Strait project is intended to contribute to reducing emissions from the islands' electricity supply.Underwater generation creates its own engineering problems. Components have to survive saltwater, strong currents and long periods of exposure while remaining accessible enough for inspection and maintenance. Getting people and equipment to a submerged turbine can also require vessels, specialist crews and careful planning. The location itself has to provide sufficient water movement, suitable depth and a practical route for sending the electricity into the grid.The Naru Strait project therefore depends on more than the turbine turning. Its subsea cable links the machine to an onshore electrical station, where the generated power can be processed for distribution. Local vessels and resources were used during deployment, with Proteus' offshore team overseeing the work, while Kyuden Mirai Energy and Japan's Ministry of Environment have been involved in advancing the project.There is also a useful way to think about the long-term promise of the machine, without treating its output as something that can be guaranteed hour by hour. The tidal timetable itself is highly predictable. Engineers can calculate when stronger and weaker currents are expected well into the future, creating a generation pattern that can be plotted ahead of time. What cannot simply be printed on that chart is the turbine's actual electricity production for every future hour: maintenance, operating conditions and other technical factors still matter.That distinction is important. The Naru Strait turbine is not a giant power station, nor does the available source material establish that it will produce a fixed amount of electricity every hour for a decade. What the project demonstrates is something more specific: a megawatt-scale machine can be installed beneath a Japanese strait, connected to shore and operated using an energy source whose basic timing is known far in advance. The water will keep changing direction. The turbine is built to follow it.
Article Summary: The AR1100 is installed in the Naru Strait near Japan’s Goto Islands. Unlike a conventional wind turbine, there is no tower standing above the water. The generating equipment works underwater, where tidal currents pass through its three-bladed rotor and turn the machinery inside the nacelle. Electricity then travels towards shore through a subsea connection.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Dwayne Johnson: "Be humble. Be hungry. And always be..." - a lesson on staying successful
Article Text:
Dwayne Johnson

Quote of the day by Dwayne Johnson

"Be humble. Be hungry. And always be the hardest worker in the room."

Dwayne Johnson’s success story is really about starting again

A simple way to actually use this idea

Other famous quotes by Dwayne Johnson

"Success isn't always about greatness. It's about consistency . Consistent hard work leads to success. Greatness will come."

. Consistent leads to success. Greatness will come." "If you have a dream, chase it. Because a dream doesn't work unless you do."

"The struggles along the way are only meant to shape you for your purpose."

Two people can reach a comparable level of success and carry themselves in completely different ways once they get there. One starts believing their own reputation, coasting on past results and expecting continued recognition without continued effort. The other keeps behaving, day to day, as though the position they've reached is still something to be earned rather than something already secured. Johnson, an actor and former professional wrestler who built one of the most consistently bankable careers in modern entertainment, has repeated some version of this line across interviews and public talks for years, treating it less as a motivational slogan and more as an operating discipline he applies to himself regardless of how much he's already accomplished. The three instructions build on each other deliberately: humility to keep success from distorting self-perception, hunger to keep ambition from going stale once a goal is reached, and outworking everyone else in the room as the concrete, checkable behaviour that proves the first two aren't just talk. His remarkable career trajectory proves that sustained success requires continuously earning respect through consistent effort, rather than simply resting on past achievements and accumulated reputation.What gives this line extra weight is how directly it maps onto Johnson's own well-documented history. Before wrestling or acting, he was cut from the Canadian Football League after a brief and unsuccessful professional football career, a setback that reportedly left him with only a few dollars to his name and forced him to move back in with his parents to rebuild from there. He then built a wrestling career from the ground up, working through years of small venues and modest paydays before becoming one of the most recognisable performers in WWE history.That same pattern repeated when he transitioned to acting, starting in supporting and low-budget roles before working his way, over roughly two decades, into becoming one of the highest-paid actors in the world. Johnson has spoken repeatedly about maintaining an intense personal work ethic, including famously early gym sessions and a demanding schedule, even at the peak of his commercial success, treating each new project as something that still has to be earned rather than something his existing fame should simply guarantee him.The useful move here is treating each of the three instructions as a separate check rather than a single vague attitude, since it's entirely possible to stay humble while quietly losing hunger, or to stay hungry while letting effort slide once recognition arrives. Humility alone can drift into complacency if nothing keeps pushing forward. Hunger alone can curdle into arrogance if nothing keeps it grounded. The third instruction, being the hardest worker in the room, is what actually forces the first two to remain honest rather than becoming things a person merely claims about themselves.A fair test, at any point success starts to feel comfortable, is to ask honestly whether the current level of effort would still hold up if nobody already knew your track record. That question won't manufacture motivation out of nothing. It usually reveals how much of the current effort is riding on reputation rather than on work still actually being done.
Article Summary: Dwayne Johnson is an actor and former professional wrestler. His quote of the day is about consistency and being the hardest worker in the room. Johnson has spoken repeatedly about maintaining an intense personal work ethic. He treats each new project as something that still has to be earned.

Article Title: Michigan man sentenced to at least 45 years after nine criminal sexual conduct convictions
Article Text:
Gerald Burton of Ishpeming, Michigan, was sentenced to three consecutive prison terms carrying a combined minimum of 45 years.

Five victims testified at May trial

Police appeal led to two new cases

Gerald Burton of Ishpeming, Michigan, was sentenced to three consecutive prison terms carrying a combined minimum of 45 years after a jury convicted him in May on nine criminal sexual conduct charges involving five victims.Marquette County Circuit Court sentenced Burton to 15 to 60 years on each of three first-degree criminal sexual conduct counts in one case, with the terms ordered to run consecutively.He was also sentenced to five to 15 years and six to 15 years in two separate cases for third-degree criminal sexual conduct by force or coercion. In a fourth case, he received 15 to 60 years for first-degree criminal sexual conduct involving injury to an incapacitated victim and one to two years each on two fourth-degree counts.A fifth case brought a 10-to-60-year sentence for first-degree criminal sexual conduct involving personal injury, according to TV6 News Team.Five victims testified at Burton's trial in May, while he maintained that all the sexual encounters had been consensual.Jurors returned their verdict after about three hours of deliberations, following closing arguments by Marquette County Prosecutor Jenna Nelson and defence attorney Karl Numinen.Numinen argued that all the encounters were consensual and that prosecutors had not proved the charges. Nelson challenged that defence in rebuttal, pointing to similarities involving the five victims.In the case involving his former girlfriend, Burton acknowledged that they had argued but denied their disputes became physical. He said he suspected infidelity and maintained that she consented when he asked her to undress and let him examine her genital area.A former co-worker testified about a November 2019 encounter, saying she and Burton had had consensual sex before that night. She said Burton forced her to perform oral sex and then raped her. Burton disputed her account and said she initiated the sexual activity.The case widened after Burton's initial arrest on felony criminal sexual conduct charges arising from two cases. The original cases carried five counts — three first-degree and two fourth-degree criminal sexual conduct charges.Police publicly sought information from others connected to the allegations after Burton's first arrest. Two other victims then contacted detectives, and Burton was later charged with one count of third-degree criminal sexual conduct in each of two new cases.After the verdict, Nelson said she hoped the outcome would encourage people to report sexual assault even years later, including those who may ask themselves, “what’s the point in coming forward now, am I going to be believed”.
Article Summary: Gerald Burton of Ishpeming, Michigan, was sentenced to three consecutive prison terms carrying a combined minimum of 45 years. He was convicted in May on nine criminal sexual conduct charges involving five victims. Five victims testified at Burton's trial in May, while he maintained that all the sexual encounters had been consensual.

Article Title: In the 1950s, US nuclear tests at Bikini and Enewetak left carbon-14 traces in Guam coral, revealing how nuclear fallout travelled across the Pacific
Article Text:
Image AI generated

Guam coral carbon-14 spikes linked to 1950s U.S. nuclear tests

How nuclear fallout carried carbon-14 into Guam coral

Guam coral reveals how nuclear fallout travelled 2,000 kilometres across the Pacific

Guam coral record helps scientists study ocean circulation and marine life

In the warm waters around Guam, a coral reef quietly recorded a series of events taking place thousands of kilometres away. During the 1950s, the United States carried out powerful thermonuclear tests at Bikini and Enewetak in the Pacific. Decades later, scientists studying a coral core from Guam found that its annual growth had preserved distinct carbon-14 changes corresponding to three of those testing campaigns. The strongest signal followed Operation Castle in 1954, while smaller rises appeared after Operation Redwing in 1956 and Operation Hardtack I in 1958. The pattern was more than a general trace of the nuclear age. The timing and shape of the peaks showed that material from the testing grounds had entered the ocean and travelled towards Guam with Pacific currents. The coral had effectively kept a chemical record of that journey, allowing scientists to reconstruct how the signal moved through the western Pacific.According to a study published in Advancing Earth and Space Sciences, titled ‘ Bomb-produced radiocarbon in the western tropical Pacific Ocean: Guam coral reveals operation-specific signals from the Pacific Proving Grounds’ , the Guam coral record contained three distinct carbon-14 spikes in 1954–55, 1956–57 and 1958–59. The researchers linked the signals to US thermonuclear testing at Bikini and Enewetak during Operations Castle, Redwing and Hardtack.As the researchers put it, “Each can be linked to thermonuclear testing” at Bikini and Enewetak.Operation Castle produced by far the strongest imprint. Six tests were conducted between late March and May 1954, with a combined yield of about 48.09 megatons. Three of the tests, Bravo, Romeo and Yankee, each exceeded 10 megatons. The later Redwing series involved 17 tests and a combined yield of about 20.8 megatons, while Hardtack I involved 31 successful tests with a combined yield of about 26.6 megatons. The latter two campaigns produced much smaller signals in the Guam coral, but they were still visible above the expected carbon-14 trend.The difference between the events is striking when the coral measurements are compared. As per NOAA, the first peak rose by roughly 700‰ above pre-bomb levels and remained elevated for about 1.2 years. The later peaks were much smaller, rising by approximately 35‰ and 70‰. Each could be linked to thermonuclear testing during the three operations. When scientists went back and sampled the relevant section at twice the original resolution, the peak was revised upwards to about 937.6 per mille, compared with the earlier value of 638.9 per mille. The higher-resolution peak occurred around September 1954.The coral did not record an explosion directly. Instead, the signal was carried into the marine environment. The researchers proposed that the intense nuclear fireballs interacted with coral reef material and the surrounding atmosphere, producing conditions capable of adding carbon-14 to material that subsequently entered the ocean. Fallout particles and carbon-containing material could then become incorporated into seawater and, eventually, into growing coral skeletons.That distinction matters because ordinary bomb-produced carbon-14 in tropical seawater behaves differently. Atmospheric carbon-14 gradually enters the ocean through air-sea exchange, producing a broad signal that is delayed and weakened compared with the atmospheric record. The Guam coral contained that expected background pattern, but the three sharp rises sat on top of it. The unusually large 1954 peak therefore pointed towards a more direct source associated with fallout from the nearby Pacific Proving Grounds.The coral itself was a Porites lobata colony from Double Reef on Guam's north-western shore. The core was collected in April 2000 and measured 273 centimetres in length. Although it contained a record stretching back to 1787, scientists concentrated on the section covering 1939 to 2000, which included the period before atmospheric nuclear testing, the rapid rise in bomb-produced carbon-14 and the later decline.The distance between the testing grounds and Guam helped make the coral record particularly useful. Bikini and Enewetak lie roughly 2,000 kilometres east of Guam, and the North Equatorial Current provided a route for material from the testing region to move westwards. The researchers found that Guam was the only coral location in their comparison where all three testing operations could be separately resolved.The timing also fitted the movement of the ocean. The carbon-14 associated with Operation Castle took roughly three months to reach Guam, travelling from the test region at an estimated average current speed of about 0.2–0.3 metres per second. The Redwing signal took around five to six months, while Hardtack I took approximately four to five months. Their smaller peaks also faded more quickly.The study went beyond simply matching dates. The researchers used ocean-current modelling to simulate how fallout particles could have travelled through different layers of the upper ocean. For Operation Castle, the model produced an arrival time at Guam that closely matched the coral record. The earliest part of the simulated signal came from relatively shallow water, although more than 60 per cent of the modelled signal came from deeper strata between 41 and 121 metres.The trail did not necessarily stop at Guam. The strongest 1954 signal was also detected in coral records elsewhere in the Pacific and was used to trace how the material could have moved through regional currents. Palau, downstream from Guam, showed a comparable early signal, while later pathways extended towards other parts of the western Pacific and the Indonesian Throughflow. The 1956 and 1958 signals, however, were not observed beyond Guam in the records examined by the researchers.The Guam coral record is useful beyond reconstructing nuclear testing. Carbon-14 preserved in coral helps scientists track ocean circulation, study the movement of bomb-produced carbon-14 through the western Pacific and estimate the ages of marine organisms. NOAA lists the Guam record as a reference dataset for these studies.The coral preserved three distinct carbon-14 signals linked to different periods of 1950s nuclear testing. The strongest signal came first, followed by two weaker ones, with their timing matching the movement of seawater from the Pacific Proving Grounds. Preserved in the coral’s annual growth layers, these signals turned the reef into a long-term natural archive of nuclear fallout and Pacific ocean history.
Article Summary: Guam coral preserved distinct carbon-14 changes corresponding to three U.S. nuclear tests. The strongest signal followed Operation Castle in 1954, while smaller rises appeared after Operation Redwing in 1956 and Operation Hardtack I in 1958. The timing and shape of the peaks showed that material from the testing grounds had entered the ocean and travelled towards Guam with Pacific currents.

Article Title: Donald Trump wins US Supreme Court nod to tighten mail voting rules before midterms
Article Text:
Mail voting faces new Trump curbs after Supreme Court sides with administration

The US Supreme Court on Monday sided with the Trump administration in a legal fight over President Donald Trump’s executive order restricting mail-in voting, clearing a procedural hurdle for the policy just weeks before states begin sending ballots for the November midterm elections.The conservative-majority court did not rule on whether Trump’s order itself is lawful. Instead, the justices ruled that the states challenging the order did not have the legal standing to bring the case. The decision allows the administration to move forward, while leaving open the possibility of fresh lawsuits that could again halt or delay implementation.“The Court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell,” the majority wrote in an unsigned order.The ruling comes with the election timetable rapidly closing in. The US Postal Service outlined plans last week for implementing Trump’s order, but some states are due to begin sending mail ballots to voters within weeks. North Carolina is scheduled to send the first mail ballots to overseas and military voters in about 10 days.“This is just the first inning of a very fast nine-inning game,” said Derek Muller, a law professor at Notre Dame University.The three liberal-leaning justices dissented from Monday’s decision, with Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson sharply criticising the ruling.Jackson wrote that the decision “lets another shoe drop in the Kafkaesque nightmare that our precedents have been steadily creating for certain plaintiffs who seek to bring election-related challenges.”New York Attorney General Letitia James described the ruling as a “painful setback” but said it would “not be the final word.”The case began after Democratic officials in 23 states and the District of Columbia challenged Trump’s executive order. They argued that the Constitution gives states and Congress authority over election administration and warned that the changes could create confusion and invite partisan abuse.“The consequences of allowing such transformative changes to take effect so close to this fall’s elections would be extreme,” attorneys for the states wrote.Dozens of state and local election officials also urged the Supreme Court to keep the order blocked while preparations for the midterms were already under way.A federal judge in Massachusetts initially blocked the policy for the states involved in that case, and an appeals court upheld her ruling. The judge later issued a second order blocking implementation nationwide, creating another obstacle for the Trump administration.The Justice Department took the case to the Supreme Court on procedural grounds in late July, arguing that the states had challenged the order prematurely. Federal lawyers also cited a separate ruling in Washington in which a judge allowed the policy to proceed.An appeals court upheld that Washington ruling while leaving open the possibility of further challenges if the administration actually implemented the changes.Federal attorneys argued that the Massachusetts ruling “blocks the government’s ability to finalize and implement the President’s proposed policies to promote election integrity for the upcoming federal elections in November.”Twelve Republican-leaning states backed the federal government before the Supreme Court, arguing that states would still have a role in determining the final voter lists.Trump signed the executive order in March as part of his broader campaign against mail-in voting. The order directs his administration to create lists of eligible voters and requires the US Postal Service to deliver mail ballots only to people included on those lists.Rules released on Friday would also prevent the Postal Service from sending mail ballots from states that do not comply with the order.Trump has repeatedly claimed that mail voting creates opportunities for fraud, despite strong evidence contradicting that claim and his own use of mail ballots. He has also blamed mail voting, without credible evidence, for his 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden.The administration has presented the new restrictions as safeguards against non-US citizens voting in federal elections. Trump has separately pushed legislation requiring voters to provide proof of citizenship.Noncitizen voting is rare and is already a felony that can carry deportation as a consequence.Mail voting has nevertheless grown increasingly popular among voters from both major parties. About 30% of all ballots cast in the 2024 presidential election were submitted by mail, according to federal data.A 2025 Brookings Institution study found roughly four cases of fraud for every 10 million mail ballots cast, highlighting the rarity of fraudulent voting through the system.Monday’s ruling was not the first recent Supreme Court decision involving Trump-backed arguments over mail voting.In June, the court ruled that states may count ballots arriving after Election Day. That case was decided after full briefing and oral arguments, rather than through the court’s emergency docket.The latest decision does not settle the broader legal dispute over Trump’s executive order. Instead, it removes the current challenge brought by the states while leaving the administration exposed to further lawsuits once implementation moves ahead.David Becker, a former Justice Department lawyer who co-wrote a book challenging Trump’s false claims about the 2020 election, said the decision created “pure chaos leading up to the midterm elections, waiting weeks after an administration filing, and just days before mail ballots go out, to compltiely rewrite the rules.”Becker said he expects Trump’s order to eventually be blocked through the new legal process opened by the Supreme Court’s decision.With the first overseas and military mail ballots expected to go out within days, the administration now has a path to begin implementing the restrictions, but the policy remains vulnerable to further legal challenges that could once again disrupt the rules before voting begins.
Article Summary: US Supreme Court sides with the Trump administration in legal fight over mail-in voting. Justices ruled that the states challenging the order did not have the legal standing to bring the case. Decision allows the administration to move forward, while leaving open the possibility of fresh lawsuits that could again halt or delay implementation.

Article Title: In 2017, Indiana’s Wolf Run Golf Course closed; after plans for 560 homes and 100,000 sq ft of shops and offices stalled, a couple paid $5.5 million for its 215 acres and helped turn it into Boone Cou
Article Text:
Jim and Nancy Carpenter bought 215 acres to save the land from development and turn it into a nature preserve. (Photo: IBJ)

From golf course to nature preserve

Couple steps in with $5.5 million

Nature quickly reclaimed the old golf course

What will Carpenter Nature Preserve look like?

Carpenters agree to sell land to Zionsville

A rare second life for a former golf course

‘It’s going to hopefully last for 100 years or more’

For years, Wolf Run Golf Club in Zionsville, Indiana, was known for its challenging fairways, water features, bunkers and rolling landscape. Today, many of those same fairways have disappeared beneath grasses and vegetation, while birds, deer, foxes, turtles and bats have returned to the property.The transformation is taking place at what is now called Carpenter Nature Preserve, named after the couple who purchased the land for $5.5 million in 2021 and helped pave the way for its future as Boone County’s largest nature preserve.Wolf Run opened in 1989 and was founded by dentist and amateur golfer Dr. Jack Leer. Designed by architect Steve Smyers, the course was known for its large water features, greenside bunkers and undulating terrain.But after nearly three decades, the golf course closed in 2017.The property's then-owner, Stan Burton, subsequently submitted plans to rezone the land for a major mixed-use development. The proposal included 360 single-family homes, 200 multifamily housing units, 50,000 square feet of retail space and 50,000 square feet of office space.When those plans stalled, Zionsville officials began looking at another possibility.Mayor Emily Styron and Deputy Mayor Julie Johns-Cole toured the former golf course with Burton, and Styron began imagining the site as a large public park.“I could start to see that this could be an amazing park for Zionsville,” Styron said.She asked Burton how much it would cost to purchase the property. His answer was $5 million.Styron began reaching out to people she believed might be interested in helping acquire the land.Among those she contacted were Jim and Nancy Carpenter, longtime Zionsville residents and owners of Wild Birds Unlimited, an Indianapolis-based franchisor with more than 300 stores selling bird feeders and bird food.Unlike a typical buyer, the Carpenters immediately saw the conservation potential of the former golf course.“When we saw [Wolf Run], we knew what would likely happen to it in the years to come for development, [and] we just couldn’t let that happen,” Nancy Carpenter said.The couple purchased the 215-acre property from Burton in 2021 for $5.5 million.The Carpenters had previously supported conservation projects, including donating land to the Brown County Nature Conservancy and contributing to a native pollinator meadow at Newfields.Their connection to wildlife made the Wolf Run opportunity particularly meaningful.Six years after the golf course closed, much of the landscape had already begun returning to nature.“The only clues that Carpenter Nature Preserve used to be Wolf Run Golf Club are the cart paths and sand traps where plants and grasses struggle to grow,” according to the Indianapolis Business Journal.The former fairways are gradually being allowed to return to woodland, while grasslands in other parts of the property are being rehabilitated to remove invasive species.Wildlife has also begun flourishing across the site.Birds, bats, deer, foxes and turtles now inhabit the former golf course. During a recent visit, an Indianapolis Business Journal reporter spotted a snapping turtle in Eagle Creek, along with orioles, blue grosbeaks, vultures and great blue herons.“This is the sixth summer, so it really takes over quickly,” Jim Carpenter said. “It’s pretty amazing what has happened, but wildlife is finding it. It’s going to be a wonderful preserve for people and nature.”The nature preserve is being developed in multiple phases.The first phase includes basic infrastructure such as trails, parking and restrooms, followed by plans for a nature center and outdoor classroom.Future development is expected to include enhanced wetlands, woodlands and prairies, boardwalks, a nature-inspired playground and overlooks along Eagle Creek.The preserve will also feature multiple ecosystems, including waterways, forests and grasslands, creating habitats for a growing range of wildlife.Zionsville Parks and Recreation Superintendent Jarod Logsdon was impressed by the site's potential when he first visited it in 2021.“My jaw dropped at the possibilities,” he said. “To have 215 acres in central Indiana is pretty unheard of.”The preserve will become the first park in rural Union Township and the largest nature preserve in Boone County.Although the property is now appraised at just over $6 million, the Carpenters agreed to sell it to the town for $4.52 million.The Zionsville Town Council voted 6-1 in May to approve a $5.5 million bond to cover the property acquisition as well as engineering, surveys and construction documents for the first phase.The town has also been nominated for several conservation grants and funding opportunities, including a potential $3 million Next Level Conservation Trust grant, a $500,000 Land and Water Conservation Fund grant and $4 million in Indiana Stream and Wetland Mitigation Program credits.Transforming a former golf course into a nature preserve is unusual. According to the Audubon Society, only a relatively small number of former golf courses across the US have been converted into preserves, wetlands or restored natural areas instead of housing and commercial developments.For the Carpenters, that rarity was precisely what made Wolf Run worth saving.“When we saw this, we recognized this is unique,” Jim Carpenter said. “You cannot find anything like this in central Indiana that will ever be available again.”As temporary caretakers, the couple has continued mowing old golf-cart paths, maintaining 24 bluebird boxes and tending two experimental pollinator gardens near the former clubhouse.The old sand traps and greens are now being viewed as opportunities for new ecosystems rather than remnants of a golf course.Nancy Carpenter said the project has not been without financial risk or stress, but believes the long-term reward will be worth it.“It’s been really, really rewarding to do a project like this,” she said. “It’s going to hopefully last for 100 years or more and provide people with joy and animals with habitat, and I hope it inspires others.”
Article Summary: Wolf Run Golf Club in Zionsville, Indiana, was known for its challenging fairways, water features, bunkers and rolling landscape. After nearly three decades, the golf course closed in 2017. The property's then-owner submitted plans to rezone the land for a major mixed-use development. Jim and Nancy Carpenter purchased the 215-acre property in 2021 for $5.5 million.

Article Title: In 1988, a retired Ohio minister received two tiny pencil sharpeners as a gift; over the next 20 years, he collected more than 3,400 and created a museum
Article Text:
World's First Pencil Sharpener Museum

How 3 pencil sharpeners became a collection of more than 3,400

Why the collection became so unusual

What happened to the collection after Johnson's death

Paul A. Johnson had just retired from the ministry in 1988 when his wife, Charlotte, gave him an unusual Christmas present: 3 tiny metal pencil sharpeners shaped like cars. The small gifts were not intended to launch a major collection, but they caught Johnson's attention and sparked a hobby that would eventually consume much of his retirement. He began searching for unusual sharpeners wherever he travelled, building a collection that grew steadily over the following decades. Flea markets, antique shops and other places became sources for new additions, and the growing display eventually outgrew the family's home. Johnson ultimately amassed more than 3,400 pencil sharpeners before his death in 2010. The collection became known as one of the largest of its kind in the United States and eventually found a permanent public home in Ohio, where thousands of the tiny objects can still be seen today.The collection began with those 3 metal car-shaped sharpeners, but Johnson soon became interested in finding examples with unusual shapes, materials and designs. According to Ohio Magazine, his collecting eventually took him to flea markets and other places where he could search for new pieces. As the number of sharpeners grew, Johnson needed more space to display them. The collection was eventually housed in a building on his property, where visitors could see the remarkable variety he had accumulated.Johnson's collection was not simply a pile of similar stationery items. It included sharpeners made from different materials and designed in an extraordinary range of forms, turning an everyday schoolroom object into something closer to miniature sculpture. The collection eventually became large enough to attract visitors, transforming what had started as a personal hobby into a curiosity that other people wanted to see.Johnson focused on manual pencil sharpeners rather than electric or battery-powered models and sought distinctive pieces rather than simply accumulating identical examples. The sharpeners represent a surprisingly broad range of subjects. Among the collection are miniature representations of animals, buildings, vehicles, landmarks and other recognisable objects, showing how manufacturers turned a basic tool into a novelty item.Johnson also organised the sharpeners into themed displays. That arrangement gave the collection a visual quality beyond its sheer size, allowing visitors to notice how differently the same basic object could be designed. Some of the pieces are particularly old, while others reflect more recent manufacturing styles. Together, they provide a quirky look at changing design trends and the enduring appeal of novelty stationery.Johnson died in 2010, but his collection was preserved rather than dispersed. It eventually became the centrepiece of the Paul A. Johnson Pencil Sharpener Museum at the Hocking Hills Regional Welcome Centre in Logan, Ohio. The museum was later moved into a new, larger facility, reopening on January 20, 2024. The new building provides improved accessibility, climate control and museum-quality display cases, giving the collection a more permanent setting.The museum now contains roughly 5,000 pencil sharpeners, combining Johnson's original collection with additional pieces that expanded the display. What makes the museum remarkable is the unlikely chain of events behind it. Three tiny metal sharpeners given as a Christmas present in 1988 eventually inspired decades of collecting and thousands of additions, turning an ordinary stationery item into the foundation of a dedicated Ohio museum.
Article Summary: Paul A. Johnson started collecting pencil sharpeners in 1988. His wife gave him 3 car-shaped pencils as a Christmas present. His collection grew steadily over the following decades. It eventually became one of the largest of its kind in the United States. Johnson died in 2010, but his collection was preserved rather than dispersed. It is now the centrepiece of a new museum in Ohio.

Article Title: US universities pausing CPT program after new ICE memo: Indian students in a fix
Article Text:
US universities are pausing CPT programs after new memo from ICE.

What did the new guideline say?

List of universities pausing CPT

UC Berkeley

UC Davis

UC San Diego, Purdue, Santa Clara

What is Day 1 CPT?

Curricular Practical Training (CPT) is a temporary work authorization that allows F-1 international students in the US to gain off-campus work experience, such as internships or co-op programs, while completing their degree. Unlike Optional Practical Training (OPT), which is approved directly by USCIS after graduation, CPT is authorized entirely by a university's Designated School Official (DSO). For CPT to be legal under federal law, the work must be an integral part of the school's established academic curriculum and directly related to the student's major. Thousands of Indian international students enrol at CPT programs every year.On August 12, 2026, the US Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP), a division of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), issued a severe compliance guidance message titled "Reminder of Liability for DSOs Regarding CPT Authorization".It said that CPT is being abused as a backdoor work permit and not actually an academic requirement. he federal warning explicitly reminded DSOs that when they sign off on a student's I-20 form for CPT, they are doing so under penalty of perjury.Improperly approving CPT endangers the individual official and risks the university losing its SEVP certification to host international students altogether.UC Berkeley announced that it would pause course credit CPT. These programs are not exactly mandatory for the course and hence this becomes a way F-1 students obtain work authorization for an off-campus internship. “Please know that we do not take this decision lightly as we know the importance that course credit CPT plays in your academic journey,” Berkeley International Office director Emmanuel said in an email sent to all international students. “We will support (international students) to the full extent allowed by law.”US Davis too acted on the ICE memo and suspended course credit or non-mandatory CPT.Both campuses specified that degree-requirement CPT -- where the training is an integral part of the curriculum-- will be processed normally.Other universities that are pausing/reconsidering CPT areDay 1 CPT is a different program that allows students to work on the very first day of the academic program. International students who lose their visa status. While Day 1 CPT was not explicitly banned, SEVP warned DSOs that they face audit risk and potential prosecution for fraud if the "required curriculum" is just a pretext to sell work authorization. These programs are now facing intense legal scrutiny and auditing.
Article Summary: Curricular Practical Training (CPT) is a temporary work authorization that allows F-1 international students in the US to gain off-campus work experience. Thousands of Indian international students enrol at CPT programs every year. On August 12, 2026, the US Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP), a division of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), issued a severe compliance guidance message.
