Article Title: 'Happy birthday wheelchair': Disabled New Jersey woman shocked seeing hurtful message on cake; restaurant says it was a reference for where the cake was to be served
Article Text:
A 29-year-old disabled woman in New Jersey gets a hurtful message on her birthday cake.

We are deeply saddened, says restaurant

29-year-old Antonia Sinibaldi, a New Jersey-based singer-songwriter, was left speechless when her birthday cake had this message: Happy birthday wheelchair or Happy wheelchair birthday -- depending on whatever way one chooses to read the unnecessary information that Sinibaldi did not need to be reminded of. Because she has been wheelchair bound since the age of 2 when she had met a road accident involving a drunk driver. She was diagnosed with a cervical spinal injury and, as a result, had to rely on a motorized wheelchair and ventilator, CBS reported.On June 20, she went out with her friends and family to celebrate her birthday at Blu On The Hudson in Weehawken."It took me by surprise," she said. "I shouldn't be reminded of something that I already know." She also said that she ordered the same thing that her cousin ordered. And the entire episode turned out to be a cruel joke on Sinibaldi.Sinibaldi said when she raised the issue with the management that wanted to send them more and more drinks.The restaurant issued an apology for the message and said it was an unfortunate mistake. "We at Blu on the Hudson are aware of the recent video circulating on social media, and we are deeply saddened by what occurred.We sincerely apologize to the guest and to everyone who was hurt or offended by this incident which took place on June 20, 2026. Treating every guest with dignity, respect, and care is fundamental to who we are as a company," they said."Our standard operating procedure is to use table and seat numbers on tickets to identify where each dish should be delivered. In this instance, the word "wheelchair" was used as a reference to identify where a birthday dessert with a candle should be delivered. Unfortunately, that notation was misunderstood and was written on the plate itself. There was absolutely no malicious or disrespectful intent behind the notation. However, we fully understand how seeing that word written on a plate could be deeply hurtful and upsetting." the statement read."Since the incident, we have reinforced with our team the importance of following proper ticketing and communication procedures and have taken steps to ensure that something like this does not happen again. We have also made an attempt to reach the guest directly to personally apologize, although we have not yet been able to connect with them," the statement added."We understand that an apology cannot undo the hurt or frustration caused by this incident, but we sincerely hope it conveys how deeply sorry we are. Blu on the Hudson is proud to be a part of the Hudson County community, and we are committed to being a place where every guest feels welcomed, respected, and valued," it said.
Article Summary: 29-year-old Antonia Sinibaldi was left speechless when her birthday cake had this message: Happy birthday wheelchair or Happy wheelchair birthday. She has been wheelchair bound since the age of 2 when she had met a road accident involving a drunk driver. The restaurant issued an apology and said it was an unfortunate mistake.

Article Title: US proposes $103,265 H-1B fee: Hiring set to become more costly
Article Text:
The higher costs of sponsoring an H-1B worker may dent hiring and could also impact the dreams of those aspiring to work in the US

The Trump administration has proposed a new $103,265 fee for cap-subject H-1B petitions, as the earlier $100,000 payment imposed through a presidential proclamation in Sept 2025 has run into legal challenges and is set to expire next month (unless extended). The new proposal, however, is based on a different legal authority and would create a separate fee regime for cap-subject H-1B petitions.The draft proposal will be open for public comments and will take a few months for finalisation and implementation.The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has proposed this new fee for every cap-subject H-1B application (termed as petition under US immigration laws) – this move will significantly raise the cost for employers seeking to hire foreign workers. It would be in addition to all existing H-1B filing and statutory fees. However, H-1B petitions that are exempt from the annual cap would not be subject to the new charge.There is an annual quota (cap) of 85,000 H-1B new visas that are allotted each year. This includes the 20,000 cap for those with advanced degrees, known as the Master’s cap. In addition, there is a cap-exempt H-1B category. Higher education institutions and related affiliated nonprofits and research organisations are among those eligible to hire cap-exempt H-1B workers.A footnote in the 67-page draft proposal indicates that the proposed fee would also not generally apply to petitions for H-1B workers who have already been counted against the annual cap and are seeking to change jobs or extend their stay.But there is a finer point – the cap exemption does not cover a worker who is eligible for a fresh six-year period of H-1B admission when the new petition (application) is filed. Thus, as the proposed $103,265 charge applies to cap-subject petitions, such a fresh six-year case could potentially attract the proposed fee.“An important point to note is that the proposed $103,265 fee is tied to whether the H-1B petition is ‘cap-subject,’ not simply to whether the worker is physically inside or outside the US,” Mitch Wexler, senior counsel at Fragomen, a global immigration law firm, told TOI.Thus, the proposed fee will not only apply to H-1Bs who were outside the US and were selected in the lottery, but will also cover students from within the US who are transiting from an F-1 visa to an H-1B.New York-based immigration attorney, Cyrus D Mehta, told TOI that: “The $103,265 fee for each cap subject H-1B is preposterous. It will also apply to F-1 students who will change status to H-1B in the US. This rule heralds the death of the H-1B program. The Trump administration has killed the goose that laid the golden eggs. The ability to attract bright and hardworking skilled workers to work for US employers and grow the economy was America's secret sauce. ”The proposed $103,265 charge is separate from the $100,000 H-1B payment introduced under a presidential proclamation announced in Sept 2025 – which applied to hiring H-1B workers from outside the US. This fee has faced legal challenges, and its implementation was vacated by a district court in June 2026, with the government's appeal still pending when the proposed rule was prepared.The Sept 2025 proclamation was originally set to expire after 12 months, so its stated expiry is in the coming month, unless extended. DHS says the proposed $103,265 fee rests on a different legal authority and is intended to create a permanent fee on cap-subject H-1B petitions.In fact, as this earlier fee typically applied to hiring H-1Bs from outside the US, the last filing season, which ended in spring, had seen an increase in hiring of immigrants within the US – such as sponsoring international students transiting from an F-1 visa. If the proposed fee, announced today, is implemented, it will dent hiring of international students, as it applies to all H-1B cap hiring.For the fiscal year ended 2025, 2.83 lakh H-1B visas were allotted to Indians – this was 70% of the total visas (including extensions). As regards new visas (for initial employment), Indians bagged nearly 58,000 visas (roughly half of the total new visas, including cap-exempt visas).Thus, the higher costs of sponsoring an H-1B worker may dent hiring and could also impact the dreams of those aspiring to work in the US.If implemented, the fee is expected to generate about $8.78 billion a year, based on an assumed 85,000 cap-subject H-1B petition number. The proposed fee would also be a major financial burden for some employers, particularly smaller companies. DHS estimates that 14,541 small entities would be affected and that 76% of them would face a cost increase exceeding 1% of annual revenue. The agency therefore acknowledges that the proposal would have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities that file cap-subject H-1B petitions. However, DHS argues that demand for H-1B workers is sufficiently strong to sustain filings at the 85,000 level even with the higher cost.Immigration experts point out that the underlying objective is to discourage hiring of immigrants rather than fee generation.
Article Summary: The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has proposed this new fee for every cap-subject H-1B application (termed as petition under US immigration laws) This move will significantly raise the cost for employers seeking to hire foreign workers. The draft proposal will be open for public comments and will take a few months for finalisation and implementation.

Article Title: In 1908, an unschooled Indiana widow began a 20-year fight to defend 120 acres of Lake Michigan dunes from a steel giant; 72 years later, 212 acres including part of her tract joined Indiana Dunes to
Article Text:
Carr remained determined to defend what she believed was hers (Photo: NPS)

How Drusilla claimed land

A party on Carr beach, 1917 (Spicerweb. org photo)

Legal fight begins

Carr continued fighting into old age

Bathhouse under construction. (Picture: Spicerweb.org)

Land becomes protected

In the early 1900s, an Indiana widow spent more than two decades fighting to defend her claim to 120 acres along Lake Michigan. Drusilla Carr had lived on the land for decades before it became valuable. As the city of Gary, Indiana, grew around her, the lakeshore that had once been seen as little more than sand and swamp became increasingly sought after for parks, homes and industry.Carr was born on July 29, 1856, in Porter County, Indiana. She and her brother became orphans during the 1860s. According to National Park Service, at the age of 13, she was recorded in the 1870 census as working as a domestic servant. The census also noted that she had never been taught to read or write.In 1872, she left that household and moved to the Lake County lakeshore near the mouth of the Grand Calumet River at Miller. She worked at a fishing shack run by John and Hank Granger. “It was near to where the Gary Marquette Park is and close to the lagoon. I cooked for them,” she later recalled.The area was then very different from the developed shoreline that exists today. It consisted mainly of sand dunes, swamps, ponds and scrub trees.Mink, muskrats and skunks were common, while raccoons, wolves and foxes were also found there. Wild rice and ducks were plentiful during the season. Carr later married Robert Carr on Christmas Day in 1875, and the couple built their life around the lake.The family depended heavily on fishing and also collected what the land and shoreline provided. Carr picked cranberries and huckleberries, gathered sassafras and collected driftwood and other wood from the beach . She also remembered how the removal of moss affected the local cranberry supply, saying, “that is the reason there are no more cranberries here.”Carr later said that in March 1876, a man named Bingham came to the area after acquiring a land claim in Section 31. According to her account, he was unhappy with the property and told her that if she moved onto it, she could have it.Carr said she copied the land description from his deed because he promised to send her a new deed later. She never saw him again and eventually stopped receiving replies from him. She continued living on the property, however, and built her life there.For years, the Carr family lived in cabins near the river and later moved closer to the lakefront. They raised children, fished and collected supplies from the surrounding land. Carr remembered one particularly large fishing haul when she and others pulled in a net containing 57 large sturgeon.The abundance did not last. Lake Michigan's native fish populations declined sharply because of overfishing. Commercial harvesting of lake sturgeon was eventually closed in 1929. The annual catch had fallen to about 2,000 pounds, compared with 3.8 million pounds in 1879.Carr also watched the landscape change as Gary developed. Around the late 1880s, the mouth of the Grand Calumet River became closed by sand. Roads were built, the Carr family moved their house and the lakeshore became more accessible.She also became acquainted with Octave Chanute, a French-American civil engineer and aviation pioneer, who used her property for early glider experiments. Townspeople reportedly called him the 'Crazy old man of the sand dunes', but Carr defended him.The situation changed significantly after Gary's construction and expansion. By 1908, the land that had once been considered remote and difficult to use had become highly valuable. Carr was 52 and a widow when the first verified legal case against her was brought.She continued to insist that the land was hers. At the same time, Gary wanted access to the Miller lakefront for a public park. The city began legal action to acquire property, but its first attempt was stopped because Miller was still a separate town and had not yet become part of Gary.The dispute continued for years. In 1911, Carr opened a bathhouse on the beach. The area became popular with visitors, and around 3,000 people reportedly visited Carr's Beach on one Sunday in 1914. The family also operated attractions and rented cottages.Carr's legal victories did not end the pressure. In 1917, Indiana's Supreme Court reversed lower court decisions that had favoured Gary's park board. In 1919, Gary eventually acquired the Town of Miller. The city then obtained lakefront land, including property connected to the Carr family's original tract.Carr remained determined to defend what she believed was hers. In 1920, she summed up her position in this statement, “No one ever told me I was on their property.”She was described by an attorney as “a forceful, determined woman with a lot of grit, although unschooled, knew her rights and would not be pushed around.”Part of Carr's land was later threatened by industrial expansion. In 1923, she made clear that she did not want the landscape around her home replaced by factories.“I hope the scenes of my youth, where I have lived so happily and brought up my children, will not be desecrated by huge industrial smoke stacks. I would rather sell to people willing to make this a beauty spot, a wonderful beach, but sell I will.”Carr also faced financial pressure during the long legal disputes. Parts of her holdings were sold to help fund the cases, while disputes over taxes and land titles continued.In 1930, she appeared in court again. A contemporary report described her as a veteran of 12 legal battles, eight of which she had won. During one hearing, when a lawyer asked whether she was too tired to continue, she replied, “Me–tired? Me? I should say not, young fellow. You go right ahead!”Carr died on September 15, 1930. At her funeral, Frederick Backemeyer described her as “a heroic little soul who stood her ground when she thought she was in the right. Strength, courage, and dignity were her clothing.”The following January, a judge ruled in favour of her estate, although Carr's heirs were required to pay back taxes and interest to establish proper ownership.The fight over Carr's land continued even after her death. In 1940, an 88-acre section of the former Carr property was sold to a land company owned by US Steel at a sheriff's sale after the estate's debts had grown.The company later decided not to use the land for industrial expansion. The property remained largely undeveloped for years as debates continued over how the Lake Michigan shoreline should be used.Marquette Park also became a focus of civil rights protests because Black residents faced discrimination and violence when trying to use its beach and recreational facilities.At the same time, there was a major debate over whether parts of the Indiana Dunes should be protected or used for industrial development and a deep-water port.By 1976, Congress was considering an expansion of the Indiana Dunes National Lakeshore. The proposed expansion included the former Carr tract between Marquette Park and land held by US Steel. The area included beaches, lagoons, ponds and black oak-blueberry forest.In 1980, US Steel donated 212 acres to the Indiana Dunes National Lakeshore. Part of that land came from Drusilla Carr's original claim, helping ensure that it would remain open space.Today, Marquette Park and Miller Woods are part of the landscape connected to Carr's story. The Paul H Douglas Trail in Miller Woods passes through beach ridges and wetlands that were once threatened by development.
Article Summary: Drusilla Carr was born on July 29, 1856, in Porter County, Indiana. She and her brother became orphans during the 1860s. At the age of 13, she was recorded as working as a domestic servant. In 1872, she left that household and moved to the Lake County lakeshore near the mouth of the Grand Calumet River at Miller.

Article Title: In 1862, heirs sold Colorado’s Baca land for 30 cents an acre; 140 years later its 97,000-acre ranch sold for $31.28 million and helped create a national park nearly four times the monument’s original
Article Text:
Photo: Baca Ranch House (clicked in 1920)Photo credit: Denver Public Library Collection via NPS

A land grant becomes an investment

The ranching years

How the Great Sand Dunes gained protection

The water-export controversy

The $31.28 million purchase

From monument to national park

Why the Baca matters today

A lesson in changing values

A piece of land can begin as a forgotten investment and end as part of a national treasure. That is the remarkable story of Colorado’s Baca Ranch, a vast property at the base of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains. In 1862, heirs of Luis María Cabeza de Baca sold the land to Territorial Governor William Gilpin for only 30 cents an acre, according to the National Park Service. More than a century later, the ranch became entangled in one of the San Luis Valley’s biggest debates: whether its groundwater should be developed and exported. As documented by the Colorado Division of Water Resources in its StreamLines newsletter, the Nature Conservancy agreed in 2002 to purchase the ranch for $31.28 million. The deal ultimately helped expand protection around the Great Sand Dunes and establish a national park and preserve.The Baca Ranch’s history began in the early nineteenth century, when the region was still under Mexican rule.In 1823, Luis María Cabeza de Baca received a large land grant from the Mexican government in what is now New Mexico. After the United States acquired control of the Southwest, the Baca claim became part of a complicated legal dispute with the federal government.Eventually, the claim was exchanged for a parcel in Colorado near the base of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains. This new property was immense, but it did not become a family homestead. In fact, no one in the Baca family ever visited the Colorado parcel, according to the National Park Service. It was treated simply as an investment.That detail gives the later conservation story an almost surprising beginning. The land that would eventually help create a national park was not initially valued for its dunes, wetlands, wildlife or water. It was an asset held at a distance, part of a legal and financial transaction whose future significance remained hidden.In 1862, the Baca heirs sold the property to William Gilpin, Colorado’s first territorial governor, for 30 cents per acre.At that price, the transaction reflected an era when vast areas of the American West were bought, sold and developed with little understanding of the ecological systems they contained. The San Luis Valley was seen largely as open land with potential for ranching, settlement and resource development.The land’s story, however, was only beginning.Cattle grazing began on the Baca property in 1862, the same year it was sold by the Baca heirs. For several years, the land was leased to different cattle owners.George Adams was the first person to develop the property fully. During the 1870s, he added fences, irrigation ditches, sheds and corrals. These improvements transformed the open tract into a more organized working ranch.The ranching era shaped the Baca’s identity for generations. It was not an untouched wilderness in the strictest sense, but a working landscape where human activity existed alongside rivers, wetlands, grasslands, mountains and dunes.That combination is important. Conservation history is sometimes told as a story of nature being protected from all human influence. The Baca offers a more complicated picture. Ranching, water management, land ownership and wildlife habitat were all woven together.The surrounding region was also extraordinary. The Great Sand Dunes rise from the floor of the San Luis Valley, backed by the rugged Sangre de Cristo Mountains. Snowmelt flows from the high country, while wind moves sand across the valley. Wetlands and groundwater help maintain the ecological conditions around the dunes.The Baca Ranch occupied a crucial position within that larger system. Its value was not limited to the acreage listed on a deed. It included the relationships between land, water and wildlife.The Great Sand Dunes were first protected as a national monument in 1932 during the administration of President Herbert Hoover.That designation was encouraged by local residents who wanted to prevent mining and other commercial activities from damaging the dunes. The campaign was led in part by women connected with local Ladies’ PEO chapters.Their efforts reflected a strong community connection to the landscape. Residents understood that the dunes were not merely a dramatic backdrop. They were a distinctive natural feature that could be permanently altered if mining and extraction expanded.The national monument protected the central dunes, but its boundaries did not encompass the entire environmental system that supported them. Over time, concerns grew about the surrounding watersheds, wetlands, groundwater and wildlife habitat.This broader perspective became particularly important in the late twentieth century, when the Baca Ranch attracted interest from water-development companies.The issue was not only whether the land itself would be built over. It was whether groundwater beneath the San Luis Valley could be pumped in enormous quantities and transported elsewhere. Local water users feared that large-scale exports could affect existing water rights, agriculture and the valley’s ecological balance.The debate changed the way many people understood the Baca. It was no longer just a large ranch near a national monument. It was part of the water system that helped sustain the region.During the late 1980s, American Water Development Inc., or AWDI, filed a water court case involving a plan to export several hundred thousand acre-feet of water from the valley to municipalities.The proposal alarmed local water users. They worried that exporting groundwater could injure their existing rights and reduce the water available for agriculture and communities.According to the Colorado Division of Water Resources newsletter, local water users successfully challenged the proposed change in water court. The legal fight illustrated how closely land ownership and water rights were connected in the San Luis Valley.The controversy did not end there. During the 1990s, the ranch changed hands, and another company, Stockman’s Water Company, pursued water development and export plans.In 1998, Stockman’s managed to place two initiatives related to its development proposal on the state ballot. Voters rejected both initiatives. Water users spent more than $1 million opposing them, showing how seriously the community viewed the threat.These battles created a turning point. If the ranch remained controlled by companies interested in water development, the valley could face renewed pressure. But if the land could be protected, it might help preserve the wider ecosystem and reduce the risk of large-scale water export.Conservation became a possible solution to a conflict that had previously been fought mainly through lawsuits, political campaigns and water regulation.In late 2000, Congress authorized the purchase of the Baca Ranch as part of an effort to create the Great Sand Dunes National Park and Preserve.The legislation provided a legal pathway for acquiring the property, but it did not make the purchase simple. The ranch was enormous, expensive and connected to years of controversy.The Nature Conservancy, which was located near both the ranch and the dunes, began negotiations to buy the property. The organization planned to acquire the ranch and then transfer it to the federal government for conservation purposes.By the end of 2001, negotiations were still moving slowly. Then another important detail emerged: the majority partner in the consortium that owned the ranch was an investment group funded by the Yale Endowment.Colorado Senator Wayne Allard met with Yale’s president and urged the university to help complete the sale. Yale agreed to donate its profits from the transaction back to the Nature Conservancy. That contribution was expected to be approximately $4 million.In January 2002, the Nature Conservancy announced that it had signed an agreement to purchase the ranch for $31.28 million. The Colorado Division of Water Resources newsletter described the property as a 100,000-acre ranch, while later National Park Service materials identify the key acquisition area as the 97,000-acre Baca Ranch.The difference in acreage likely reflects how the property and transferred lands were described at different stages of the transaction. The central point remains the same: a vast ranch was secured for conservation at a cost of more than $31 million.Compared with the 30 cents per acre paid by William Gilpin in 1862, the later sale represented a dramatic change in financial value. But the real transformation was not simply monetary. The land had acquired a new kind of value—one based on ecological protection, public benefit and cultural significance.The Baca purchase helped make possible the expansion of Great Sand Dunes National Monument into Great Sand Dunes National Park and Preserve.The new designation was officially created in September 2004, after the federal government completed the purchase and transfer process. The expansion made the protected area nearly four times larger than the original monument.The newly protected landscape included more than the famous dunes. It contained wetlands, wildlife habitat, archaeological sites, grasslands and important portions of the surrounding watershed.Some of the Baca lands were incorporated into the national park, while other parts became the Baca National Wildlife Refuge. The refuge was created next to the park and added another layer of protection for wildlife and habitat.The park and preserve also encompass higher-elevation environments, including forests, alpine tundra, lakes and streams. These areas are connected to the dunes through water and climate. Snow that falls in the mountains can eventually contribute to streams and groundwater in the valley below.Protecting the high country and the valley floor together created a more complete conservation landscape.The National Park Service explains that the Baca Ranch helped protect resources vital to the Great Sand Dunes. Without the acquisition, the national monument would have remained more isolated from the ecosystems that influence its survival.The Baca Ranch story shows why conservation cannot always be limited to the most visually impressive feature in a landscape.The dunes attract attention because they are spectacular. Their towering ridges of sand appear almost otherworldly against the Colorado mountains. But the dunes are sustained by less obvious processes involving wind, streams, snowmelt, groundwater and wetlands.If those surrounding systems are disrupted, the dunes could be affected even if the most recognizable sand formations remain protected.The Baca acquisition helped preserve those connections. It also protected habitat for birds and other wildlife, along with archaeological and cultural resources that reflect the long human history of the San Luis Valley.The story also demonstrates the importance of local communities in conservation. Residents challenged water-export proposals, defended their water rights and pushed back against development plans. Their efforts helped create the political environment in which national protection became possible.Government agencies, conservation groups, elected officials and private institutions each played a role. No single organization could have completed the effort alone.In 1862, the Baca land was sold for a price that now seems astonishingly low. More than 140 years later, the ranch was purchased for $31.28 million and became part of a national conservation achievement.The contrast is tempting to describe as a simple real-estate story: land bought cheaply and sold for far more. But that interpretation misses the deeper meaning.The ranch’s importance did not come only from its market price. Its value grew as people understood the water, wildlife and cultural systems connected to it. What had once appeared to be an isolated investment became essential to protecting one of the country’s most unusual landscapes.The Baca also reminds us that preservation often happens just before a landscape reaches a point of no return. Had water-development plans succeeded, the effects on the San Luis Valley might have been difficult to reverse. Purchasing the ranch created a chance to protect the land before large-scale extraction changed its future.Today, visitors may see the Great Sand Dunes as a place for hiking, photography, sandboarding and quiet reflection. Behind that experience lies a long history of legal disputes, ranching, community activism and conservation negotiations.The dunes may be the most visible part of the story, but the Baca Ranch is what helped give that story a larger and more secure future.
Article Summary: In 1862, Luis María Cabeza de Baca sold the land to Territorial Governor William Gilpin for only 30 cents an acre. More than a century later, the ranch became entangled in one of the San Luis Valley’s biggest debates. The Nature Conservancy agreed in 2002 to purchase the ranch for $31.28 million. The deal ultimately helped expand protection around the Great Sand Dunes.

Article Title: 'Nothing changes yet': Immigration lawyer explains new $103,265 H-1B fee rule is not final; there will be litigation
Article Text:
Immigration attorney explains the new H-1B fee proposal.

$100k H-1B visa fee

$103,265 H-1B visa fee

The Donald Trump administration dropped another H-1B bombshell Monday as it tweaked the $100,000 H-1B fee and issued a draft rule increasing the fee to $103,265. The increase is not the main issue of the new proposal; in the new proposal, every H-1B petition will have to pay this fee, while the earlier $100K was meant for only those who needed to undergo consular processing. This means that the earlier fee was not applicable to those who were already in the US and got selected in the H-1B lottery. But the new proposal says everyone will have to pay the new fee if they are picked by the lottery.Immigration attorney Emily Neumann said it is part of the playbook which believes in throwing enough things at the wall so that something might stick. But this would not stick, Neumann said, explaining that if it becomes final, there will be litigation.In September 2025, Donald Trump signed an executive order bringing in a $100K fee on H-1B visas. The companies were supposed to pay it for every petition they file. Several lawsuits were filed against the fee and it was vacated by the court.As things stand now, for H-1Bs who will join the US workforce from October 1, FY 2027, the companies did not have to pay the fee as courts had blocked the fee. On June 8, 2026, a federal judge in Massachusetts ruled that the $100,000 fee requirement was an unlawful tax.: On July 24, 2026, the First Circuit Court of Appeals formally denied the federal government's request to resume collecting the fee while the appeal proceeds.On August 24, the Department of Homeland Security proposed an increased fee with an expansion of scope. All H-1B workers subject to the annual statutory cap, including those with master's degrees, will come under the new fee. Those who studied in the US, those who already worked in the US would also not be spared from the fee.Neumann said that this time they are using a different statutory authority. "Same number. New wrapper. Same playbook. Throw enough things at the wall to restrict legal immigration and eventually something might stick (this won't). For now, it is only a proposal. Nothing changes yet. And it would apply only to new H-1Bs selected in next year’s cap lottery. There will be a comment period. If it becomes final, there will be litigation," Neumann said.
Article Summary: The Donald Trump administration tweaked the $100,000 H-1B fee and issued a draft rule increasing the fee to $103,265. The earlier $100K was meant for only those who needed to undergo consular processing. The new proposal says everyone will have to pay the new fee if they are picked by the lottery.

Article Title: The Oval Obese: Trump's junk food habit crashes into Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) crusade
Article Text:
US stuck between Make America Healthy Again and a President fond of junk food

The TOI correspondent from Washington:

The United States once had a president who got stuck in a bathtub. It now has one who may be in danger of getting stuck between two stools: the White House’s “Make America Healthy Again” campaign on one side and Donald Trump’s famously unhealthy relationship with fast food on the other.William Howard Taft, America’s 27th president, remains the heavyweight champion of the Oval Office. At roughly 335-340 pounds, Taft was so large that a legendary tale has him becoming wedged in the White House bathtub. The story probably doesn’t hold water — historians think it was political tub-thumping — but records note that the White House did indeed commission a special seven-foot- plus “Taft tub”, and a contemporary photograph shows four men sitting comfortably inside it.Trump has yet to encounter any comparable plumbing issue, either in the White House bathrooms – some of which he has redesigned – or in his blood vessels. But the president has had his own weighty moments in history. In 2019, at a reported 243lbs and 6-foot-3, he had a Body Mass Index (BMI) of 30.4, technically putting him in the obese category.Other reports put him at much less - for instance when he was charged in Georgia in an election interference case, his booking record listed his weight as 215 lbs.Another report in April 2025 put him at 224 lbs, with a BMI of 28 — overweight, but not obese. But as per a medical report released by the White House and cited by the Washington Post, in May this year he weighed 238 pounds.In all instances, the White House -- and Trump himself -- insists he is in the pink of health. Still, doctors are now warning that the president’s waistline deserves more attention than his usual waistcoat-and-tie camouflage, maintaining that obesity should be a presidential health priority akin to protecting the commander in chief from physical threats.Trump, naturally, has never been one to let calories stand between him and a photo -- or potato -- opportunity. His culinary preferences are less farm-to-table than table-to mouth: McDonald’s, burgers, fries, steak and Diet Coke. His affection for fast food has long been a staple of the comedy circuit, with late-night hosts routinely feasting on the president’s diet. Although one comedian joked that Trump has “the thinnest fat skin of any human,” weight is one area where the President has cheerfully embraced the jibes, once telling a reporter that he has “good genes” and his habits might not matter much.More recently, he has been even more Trumpian about it. Discussing advice from Mehmet Oz -- a TV presenter who is also the administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services -- to lose weight, he joked: “I went on his show and he determined that I should lose weight," adding that he told Oz, “I don’t need you saying that in front of millions of people.”This is where the White House menu gets deliciously contradictory. Trump’s Health Secretary Robert Kennedy has made “Make America Healthy Again” the administration’s dietary gospel. His campaign urges Americans to eat “real food,” cut down on ultra-processed products and sugary drinks, and emphasize nutritious, minimally processed meals. Kennedy recently launched a program encouraging hospitals to replace deep-fried and ultra-processed fare with healthier food. In other words, Kennedy wants America to put down the fries while Trump is busy handing them out.Trump has demonstrated his culinary populism by serving burgers and fries on several occasions at the White House, whole his preference for burgers and coke are frequently on display. The president and his health secretary thus appear to be conducting a curious two-man experiment: one is telling America to eat its vegetables while the other is disdaining them.The contradiction is not merely comic; America has a serious weight problem. Federal health officials say six in 10 Americans have at least one chronic condition, while roughly 40% are diabetic or prediabetic. So perhaps the greatest challenge for MAHA is not just getting Americans to eat better; It is getting its most famous principal to lead by example. Fat chance, in the eyes of most Trump watchers.
Article Summary: Donald Trump has a BMI of 30.4, technically putting him in the obese category. At a reported 243lbs and 6-foot-3, he had a reported BMI of 238lbs in May this year. Trump’s Health Secretary Robert Kennedy has made “Make America Healthy Again’ the administration's dietary gospel. Kennedy wants America to put down the fries while Trump is busy handing them out.

Article Title: Meet Finley Holz, the Minnesota student who studied 10 years of wolf-tracking data and found deep snow can make wolves move less
Article Text:
Image AI generated

How Finley Holz used wolf-tracking and winter weather data to study wolf movement

Image AI generated

Deep snow was linked to reduced wolf movement in Minnesota

Finley Holz found wolf movement decreased as winter storms approached

Finley Holz’s wolf research earns second place in Minnesota Story Map competition

Minnesota student’s decade-long wolf research reveals effects of snow and storms

Holz combined wolf-tracking records with winter weather data, including temperature, snow depth and snowfall. Using ArcGIS Pro, he mapped wolf locations and converted them into movement data, while a Python programme helped compare movements with weather conditions. His research found that deeper snow was linked to reduced wolf movement. The study recorded a statistically significant negative correlation between snow depth and movement.However, cold snaps did not significantly affect how much the wolves moved. The research also produced an unexpected finding. Wolf movement decreased as a winter storm approached, while three days after a storm, movement was significantly below the average winter level. Holz's project was recognised in a Minnesota Story Map competition, where he placed second.Holz combined wolf-tracking information with winter weather measurements, including high and low temperatures, snow depth and snowfall events.The project used ArcGIS Pro to organise shapefiles and create maps showing wolf locations. The resulting location points were then converted into movement data. Holz also wrote a Python programme to align the wolf movements with the different winter weather conditions.The data came from wolf collar information provided by the Fond du Lac Resource Management Division. Pine Knot News, a Minnesota-based publication, reports that wildlife programme manager Michael Schrage provided wolf collar data and guidance to the students. Holz and other students also had the opportunity to collar Otter Creek wolf pups on the Fond du Lac Reservation on 5 May.One of the clearest findings from Holz's research was the relationship between snow depth and wolf movement. According to the project published in Fairfolio, titled ‘ The Effect of Winter Weather Events on Wolf (Canis lupus) Movement on the Fond du Lac Reservation’ , Holz's second hypothesis was supported: wolves moved less as snow depth increased. The study found a statistically significant negative correlation between snow depth and wolf movement. In simple terms, the data showed that as the snow became deeper, the distance wolves travelled per movement decreased.The finding in similar terms, stating that Holz "found that winter cold snaps have no effect on wolf movement" but that there was "a negative correlation between snow depth and wolf movement: the deeper the snow, the less the wolves moved." Holz had also expected extreme cold to affect wolf movement. His third hypothesis predicted that wolves would move the least during a cold snap. However, the results did not support this idea. The Fairfolio project says there was no difference in wolf movement during a cold snap compared with normal winter movement. That meant that extremely cold periods, at least within the conditions examined in the study, did not produce the reduction in movement Holz had expected.Another unexpected finding came from the relationship between wolf movement and winter storms. Holz originally hypothesised that wolves would travel the furthest immediately after a storm. Instead, the data showed that their movement declined around the time of a storm.According to the project abstract, "Three days after the storm had passed, the wolves moved significantly less than the average winter movement (p<.001)." After that period, their movement returned to the normal winter pattern. The study also found something Holz described as surprising: wolf movement decreased each day as a winter storm approached.The project says this "appears to indicate that the wolves were able to sense the oncoming storm before it arrived."Holz's wolf research also became part of a successful Minnesota Story Map competition. Two Cloquet High School students and a Hermantown student with Cloquet connections won the top three places in the competition. Hermantown freshman Gabriel Bradley came first, while Cloquet sophomores Finley Holz and Melanie Buhs placed second and third.The Minnesota Alliance for Geographic Education competition challenges students to conduct research and present their findings through an ArcGIS Online story map.Holz's project focused on the effect of winter weather events on wolf movement, while Bradley's project examined factors affecting wolf pack den relocation.Holz's project provides a detailed look at how winter conditions can influence wolf movement in northeastern Minnesota. Rather than finding that every form of severe winter weather caused wolves to travel less, the research showed a more specific pattern. Increasing snow depth was associated with reduced wolf movement, while cold snaps alone did not significantly change movement.The study also raised a new question about how wolves respond to approaching storms. The observation that movement decreased before a storm arrived suggests that further research could investigate whether wolves respond to changes in atmospheric or environmental conditions before severe weather reaches the area.For a high-school research project, Holz's work combined a decade of wildlife-tracking information with geographic mapping, weather data and computer analysis to examine the behaviour of an important northern predator.
Article Summary: Finley Holz combined wolf-tracking and winter weather data to study wolf movement in Minnesota. He found that deeper snow was linked to reduced wolf movement. Wolf movement decreased as a winter storm approached, while three days after a storm, movement was significantly below the average winter level.

Article Title: Albany Police Department issues BOLO for a man who picked $30 from the floor while shopping at Walmart; faces backlash, says no charges will be filed
Article Text:
Albany Police Department became a laughing stock when it issued a BOLO notice for a man who picked up $30 from the floor while shopping at Walmart.

No charges will be filed

The Albany Police Department issued a Be on the Lookout order for a man who apparently picked up $30 from the floor while shopping at Walmart. Sharing a surveillance photo of the man, the police department sought public help in identifying him. Social media made fun of the police department and stood strongly by the unidentified man and said nobody will be snitching about the man even if they know him over $30."The Albany Police Department would like the public's assistance with identifying the suspect in the photo. The incident occurred at 2586 N. Slappey Blvd. (Walmart). An individual dropped $30.00 on the ground while shopping. This individual picked up the money and did not turn it in to the employees. Anyone with information that may assist with identifying this individual is asked to contact the Albany Police Department at 229-431-2100," the department's original post said.Facebook users asked what exactly the crime of the man was. "I'll cover the 30.00 leave the old guy alone," one said. "Imagine finding $30 and thinking it is your lucky day, only need to go home and load up Facebook to find your photo on the police departments page asking for assistance identifying you," another wrote.Many social media users asked whether it was joke because they could not bring themselves to believe that the police department was ready to use any resource to find $30 and the man behind it."So when I find pennies and quarters on the ground, who do I turn them in to?" one wrote. "So is my toddler going to get arrested for picking up change he finds too????" a mother thought out loud. "Yall acting like he took it out someone’s pocket or stole it," one added.After the police's BOLO notice went viral, the department provided an update that the man in the photo returned the money to the victim. "The victim initially wished to pursue charges, but after the money was returned, advised that they no longer wished to press charges. No charges will be filed," the department said triggering reactions from Albany residents whether all other crime cases were solved.
Article Summary: Albany Police Department issued a Be on the Lookout order for a man who apparently picked up $30 from the floor while shopping at Walmart. Social media made fun of the police department and stood strongly by the unidentified man. "I'll cover the 30.00 leave the old guy alone," one said.

Article Title: In 1988, Arthur creator Marc Brown bought a Martha’s Vineyard estate for $700,000; after 37 years and writing half the books there, he sold it for $6.4 million
Article Text:
Martha’s Vineyard estate (Image Credit: Instagram/ @wsjrealestate)

A 37-year connection

Martha’s Vineyard estate sold for $6.4 million (Image Credit: Instagram/ @wsjrealestate)

Years of restoration

From $700,000 to $6.4 million

A home with a creative legacy

Arthur creator Marc Brown and his wife, artist Laurene “Laurie” Krasny Brown, have sold their longtime Martha’s Vineyard estate for $6.4 million after spending decades restoring the property. As reported by The Wall Street Journal, the 7.8-acre Vineyard Haven property sold after being listed for $6.9 million in 2025 and later reduced to $6.495 million before going under contract in June 2026. The couple spent years and millions of dollars renovating the estate, which became both a family retreat and an important part of Brown’s creative life.Brown and Laurie first bought the property in 1988 for $700,000, according to property records cited by PEOPLE. They went on to own the estate for 37 years, gradually restoring its historic buildings while retaining its character. The property dates to the 1730s and was once part of a much larger 225-acre farm.The estate became more than a vacation home for the couple. It was also a place where their artistic work could flourish. Brown, who created the aardvark character Arthur and built the popular children's book series around him, used the property as a creative retreat away from the couple's primary residence in New York City.The connection to Arthur is particularly significant. Brown told The Wall Street Journal that he wrote about half of the Arthur books at the Martha's Vineyard property.That detail gives the estate a unique place in the history of the children's series. While millions of readers know Arthur as the fictional aardvark at the centre of the books and television series, a substantial part of the character's literary history was created at this private island retreat.The Browns did not leave the historic estate unchanged. Over more than three decades, they invested considerable time and money restoring and renovating the property. The couple spent millions of dollars on the work, with Brown and Laurie approaching the property from an artistic perspective. The result is a collection of spaces that combine the property's historic character with additions designed for modern family life and creative work. According to PEOPLE, the main residence is a renovated antique farmhouse with five bedrooms and four bathrooms. The property also includes a saltwater swimming pool, a two-bedroom pool house and a carriage house with an artist studio above a three-car garage. There are two artist studios on the estate in total.For the Browns, those creative spaces were an important part of the property's identity. Their work as artists shaped how they approached the restoration; the couple viewed the setting almost like a composition that could continually be refined.The property's final sale price represents a significant increase from the $700,000 the Browns paid in 1988. However, the difference should be viewed alongside the substantial investment they made in restoring the estate over the years. The couple initially put the property on the market in July 2025 for $6.9 million. The asking price was later reduced to $6.495 million before the property went into contract in June 2026. It ultimately sold for $6.4 million.The sale also marks a change in direction for the couple. Rather than simply leaving Martha's Vineyard, they are turning their attention to another restoration project. PEOPLE reported that Brown and Laurie recently purchased a home in New York's Hudson Valley that they plan to restore.For nearly four decades, the Martha's Vineyard estate served several purposes for Brown and his wife. It was a vacation home, a restoration project and a place where their artistic careers developed alongside one another. Its connection to Arthur, however, may be what makes the property particularly memorable. Half of the books featuring the beloved aardvark were written there, meaning the estate became part of the creative story behind a series that went on to become a major children's franchise.Now the property has a new owner, bringing Brown's 37-year chapter on Martha's Vineyard to an end. The $6.4 million sale closes the story of a home that the couple spent decades restoring, while the next chapter of their life will involve another historic property and another restoration project in New York's Hudson Valley.
Article Summary: The 7.8-acre Vineyard Haven property sold after being listed for $6.9 million in 2025. The asking price was later reduced to $ 6.495 million before going under contract in June 2026. The couple spent years and millions of dollars renovating the estate, which became both a family retreat and an important part of Brown's creative life. Half of the books featuring the beloved aardvark were written there.

Article Title: ‘CTA intentionally prevented’: PTI alleges negligence over Imran Khan’s hospital visit
Article Text:
Imran Khan’s medical care under scrutiny

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think the inquiry committee established by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif will lead to accountability? Yes, it will No, it won't 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), the party of former Prime Minister Imran Khan, on Monday criticised what it called the “continued failure” of authorities at a state-run hospital, alleging that a CT Coronary Angiography (CTA) scheduled for Khan was not conducted despite cardiologists warning of potential cardiac complications.In a statement on Sunday, PTI central secretary Information Sheikh Waqas Akram said authorities had failed to provide the 73-year-old Khan with the medically recommended diagnostic test despite a functional CT scanner being available at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS), Dawn reported."This cannot be dismissed as an isolated administrative lapse; it reflects a deeply troubling pattern,” Akram said.Akram also cited a Supreme Court order directing Khan to undergo a comprehensive medical examination and treatment at Shifa International Hospital.He alleged that authorities had bypassed the directive and instead transferred Khan to a facility where the CT angiography was not conducted.“When the necessary facilities were available at Shifa International, deliberately taking Khan to a hospital unable or unwilling to perform the procedure raises a grave question: was the decision made in advance to prevent the CT Coronary Angiography from being conducted?” he asked."Even the government’s own doctors considered this diagnostic test necessary,” Akram added.Akram said a government medical board examined Khan on August 10 after he complained of heart palpitations and severe headaches.He said a cardiologist at PIMS had recommended a CTA on August 1 after Khan experienced fluctuating blood pressure and restlessness, citing potential cardiac complications given his age and prolonged isolation.Taking note of the reports, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday formed an inquiry committee, headed by the Establishment Division secretary, to establish the facts and determine responsibility.Commenting on the Prime Minister’s decision to constitute an inquiry committee following reports that Imran Khan’s CTA was not conducted, Akram said the move raised “serious questions as to why the medically recommended test was not conducted in the first instance. Why coordination between the cardiology and radiology departments had failed, and why Imran Khan was not taken to Shifa International despite the availability of the required facilities there”."Imran Khan’s heart health cannot be subjected to political calculations, administrative excuses or further delay,” Akram said."Political victimisation must never be permitted to endanger a human life through the denial or postponement of essential medical care. The decision to take him to a facility where the required test was not conducted, despite the availability of the necessary facilities at Shifa International, has created serious concerns that the procedure was intentionally prevented,” he alleged."The government and all relevant authorities will bear full responsibility for any further deterioration in his condition,” Akram added.Meanwhile, former India captains Sunil Gavaskar, Kapil Dev and Dilip Vengsarkar are among 21 former international cricket captains who have written to Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, urging authorities to ensure proper medical treatment and the welfare of Imran Khan.The letter, initiated by former Australia captain Greg Chappell, marks the second appeal by former international cricketers calling for humane treatment and adequate medical care for the 73-year-old Khan.Khan was arrested on August 5, 2023, in connection with a corruption case and has remained in custody since then. He is currently lodged in Adiala Jail, a detention facility on the outskirts of Rawalpindi.Khan’s relatives and supporters have repeatedly alleged human rights violations and accused authorities of restricting his access to adequate medical care, family visits and legal counsel.
Article Summary: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), the party of former Prime Minister Imran Khan, on Monday criticised what it called the “continued failure” of authorities at a state-run hospital. PTI alleges that a CT Coronary Angiography (CTA) scheduled for Khan was not conducted despite cardiologists warning of potential cardiac complications. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday formed an inquiry committee, headed by the Establishment Division secretary.

Article Title: ‘You are powerful, but remember 1971?’ Pakistani politician takes fresh swipe at Army
Article Text:
Fazlur Rehman (File photo)

(With ANI inputs)

Pakistani politician and Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam (F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman continued his verbal attacks on the Pakistan Army, recalling the military's decisive defeat in the 1971 war with India that led to the creation of Bangladesh, then known as East Pakistan.“‘We are the protectors of this country. No one’s father can harm this country.’ I agree, you are very powerful,” Rehman remarked at a JUI (F) convention in Peshawar, targeting Pakistan’s top military leadership.He recalled how the Pakistan Army laid down its arms in 1971, just a day after then-President and military ruler General Yahya Khan declared that it would fight until the end."But I remember, and maybe there are some elders who remember, that in December 1971, one day before laying down arms, General Yahya Khan addressed the army and said, we will fight in the streets, in the deserts, in the fields, in the factories, in the mountains, and we will fight against them. We will fight. We heard these big words then," Rehman added.The JUI-F further chief questioned why the public is being subjected to "severe hardships" while the establishment remains "insensitive" to their misery.“Why are you putting the country and the people to the test? Why are you having fun when your public is suffering? And today is 2026. When the revolution came in Afghanistan in 1989, and the war started, now you tell me, it’s been 45-46 years, blood has been flowing on the same line for about half a century.When blood flows like this, then it is a sign of geographical changes,” Rehman remarked.Warning that persistent state oppression and ongoing conflict threaten the nation’s integrity and could signal territorial disintegration, he stated, “It is a sign of oppression. Then at least inform us of your intentions. We are tolerating it and will continue to tolerate it. It will continue. A few more days, my dear, just a few more days. We are forced to take a breath in the shade of oppression. If we endure the oppression for a little longer, if we suffer, if we cry, it is the legacy of our ancestors. We are helpless.”Rehman’s remarks came days after he challenged the military to enter politics directly, declaring, “If you want to do politics, then take off the uniform and come; participate in the elections, and it will become clear what votes people give to those in uniform. It is your prerogative to give government to whomever you want, and to snatch it away from whomever you wish.”
Article Summary: Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam (F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman continued his verbal attacks on the Pakistan Army. He recalled the military's decisive defeat in the 1971 war with India that led to the creation of Bangladesh. He questioned why the public is being subjected to "severe hardships" while the establishment remains "insensitive"

Article Title: Pakistan: Security official killed by unidentified gunmen; 5 cops injured in separate grenade blast
Article Text:
According to police, two unidentified armed men targeted the security official. (Photo credit: IANS)

Five policemen injured in grenade attack

A security official was killed on Sunday after unidentified gunmen opened fire in northwest Pakistan, police said, according to news agency PTI.The incident took place within the jurisdiction of Badaber Police Station on the outskirts of Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.According to police, two unidentified armed men riding a motorcycle targeted the official, who was posted with the Counter Terrorism Department.He was killed on the spot, while the assailants fled the scene following the attack. Police cordoned off the area and launched a search operation to trace the attackers.No individual or group has so far claimed responsibility for the attack.In a separate incident in Mohmand district, five policemen were injured when two unidentified men hurled a hand grenade at a police post in Ambar tehsil, police said.Police retaliated with gunfire, forcing the attackers to flee. The injured policemen were taken to a nearby hospital and are said to be out of danger. An investigation is underway.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which borders Afghanistan, has witnessed recurring militant violence, cross-border movement of fighters and military operations.Pakistan's federal government has blamed the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) for attacks in areas bordering Afghanistan since a ceasefire agreement between the two sides ended in November 2022.
Article Summary: A security official was killed on Sunday after unidentified gunmen opened fire in northwest Pakistan. In a separate incident, five policemen were injured when two unidentified men hurled a hand grenade at a police post in Ambar tehsil. The injured policemen were taken to a nearby hospital and are said to be out of danger.

Article Title: Destroyed in Operation Sindoor, JeM's Bahawalpur terror base fully operational again
Article Text:
Intelligence reports indicate that Pakistani authorities channeled 250 million PKR in cash to JeM,

Fresh footage indicates it is fully operational again, complete with reconstructed domes.

ALSO READ |

NEW DELHI: Extensive restoration work has concluded at the Markaz Subhanallah facility, the primary base for the UN-sanctioned terrorist group Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM), a little over a year after the compound suffered severe structural destruction during India's Operation Sindoor retaliatory strikes.Fresh footage indicates it is fully operational again, complete with reconstructed domes, updated interior plastering, new paint, and premium marble flooring that conceals previous blast damage.Deep blast zones within the primary hall were filled with concrete, while ruined satellite buildings—including the Al-Sabir seminary and housing units for leadership—were demolished to enable new construction.Intelligence reports indicate that Pakistani authorities channeled 250 million PKR in cash to JeM, with approximately 110 million PKR dedicated specifically to restoring the central complex over a 15-month period.With JeM leader Masood Azhar incapacitated by health issues, day-to-day command of the Bahawalpur facility has shifted to his brothers, Talha Al-Saif and Mohinuddin Aurangzeb (also known as Ammar Alvi).Meanwhile, senior figures Masood Azhar and Rauf Asghar remain harbored under government protection in the Nawabshah district of Sindh, sources said.
Article Summary: Extensive restoration work has concluded at the Markaz Subhanallah facility, the primary base for the UN-sanctioned terrorist group Jaish-e-Mohammed. The compound suffered severe structural destruction during India's Operation Sindoor retaliatory strikes.

Article Title: Pakistan power crisis: Karachi residents riot amid outages lasting hours, block major roads
Article Text:
Protesters blocked major roads and intersections, burned tyres and clashed with K-Electric personnel over prolonged blackouts (ANI photo)

Power protests erupted across several parts of Karachi as residents took to the streets over prolonged and unannounced outages, blocking major roads and burning tyres while demanding restoration of electricity.Demonstrations were reported in Pak Colony, Liaquatabad, Gharibabad, Nishtar Road, Bhimpura and Ranchore Line, disrupting traffic across key parts of Pakistan’s commercial capital. In Liaquatabad, protesters blocked major intersections, while clashes between traders and K-Electric (KE) staff over outages escalated into tyre-burning on Nishtar Road, as reported by local news outle Dawn.Residents said they were facing 12 hours or more of daily power cuts, often without adequate notice. The outages have also disrupted water supplies as pumping stations remain shut when electricity is unavailable, adding to public anger.“Bill-paying citizens are being punished with 12-hour load-shedding,” a protester in Liaquatabad said.The crisis also hit businesses and households, with residents reporting spoiled food, disrupted studies and sleepless nights as fans remained unusable during blackouts.The protests compounded an already severe traffic situation in the city. Roads were also closed for traditional Chup Tazia processions, while the power protests triggered additional blockades. Traffic police diverted vehicles to alternative routes, but those too became congested.Asif Khan, a private-sector employee, told Dawn he took four hours to travel from SITE to Liaquatabad after leaving work around 5pm. Another commuter said an ambulance carrying his feverish mother was stuck for about two hours near Civic Centre while they were travelling to a doctor in Saddar.“We pay bills on time but still face 12-hour power outages. Today we couldn’t even reach home,” commuter Imran from Gharibabad said.KE, however, attributed the prolonged outages in some affected areas to electricity theft and unpaid bills. A company spokesperson said outstanding dues from defaulters in Bandhani Colony and Rexer Line had crossed PKR 3 billion, adding that the duration of load-shedding depended on “electricity theft and the level of losses in the area”.The protests come as Karachi continues to grapple with an electricity crisis that is also affecting water supply, businesses and daily life across densely populated neighbourhoods.
Article Summary: Demonstrations reported in Pak Colony, Liaquatabad, Gharibabad, Nishtar Road, Bhimpura and Ranchore Line. Protesters blocked major roads and intersections, burned tyres and clashed with K-Electric personnel. Residents said they were facing 12 hours or more of daily power cuts, often without adequate notice.

Article Title: 'India could use water as weapon': Pakistan minister as Indus Waters Treaty remains in abeyance
Article Text:
Pakistan minister Ahsan Iqbal (File photo)

Pakistan minister Ahsan Iqbal has said India could “weaponise” the Indus Water Treaty (IWT) and expressed hope that “better sense” would prevail to prevent the two neighbours from going to war again, this time over water.He noted that the treaty had remained “untouchable” for almost seven decades since it was signed in 1960, but New Delhi has now been kept in abeyance “unilaterally."“...Indus Water Treaty that has stood the test of time for the last 70 years. India and Pakistan fought several wars, but it (IWT) was considered untouchable because it is an international agreement, and this time around the Indian government has unilaterally held it in abeyance... first time probably water has been weaponised in history,” Iqbal told the Asia Society.“We (Pakistan) now face this threat that they (India) can use water as a weapon to deny Pakistan when it needs it for its crops and release it when we don't need it... We are using all the diplomatic means to make sure that we don't have future wars on water because we have already seen lots of wars,” the minister added.He further stated that South Asian countries should instead focus on issues such as development, poverty, illiteracy and the youth “bulge”, describing the region as the “least integrated” in the world."So we hope that there is better sense in our neighbour's (India) mind and we don't see that water is weaponised and we go to another conflict with India over water because Pakistan cannot surrender at any cost the future of its 250 million people for its food security and right of water. If we let it happen, then every state that is on the lower side of water supply would be hostage to any country that controls the rivers," the Pakistan Muslim League (Nawaz) leader remarked.Iqbal's remarks came days after Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif warned India of a “direct response” for putting the IWT in abeyance.“India proved itself an enemy of peace by unilaterally and illegally suspending the Indus Waters Treaty. I declare in clear terms that every single drop of Pakistan's water is our red line. If India does not come to its senses, it will be responded to directly,” Sharif said on August 13, on the eve of Pakistan's Independence Day.New Delhi put the agreement in abeyance following the Pahalgam terror attack in April last year. Since then, Pakistani leaders have repeatedly called water their “red line” and threatened India over the move, describing it as an “act of war.”
Article Summary: Ahsan Iqbal says India could use water as a weapon to deny Pakistan when it needs it for its crops. New Delhi put the agreement in abeyance following the Pahalgam terror attack in April last year. Pakistani leaders have repeatedly called water their “red line” and threatened India.

Article Title: ‘In contempt for gathering people’: Pak blames ex PM Imran Khan’s party for hospital transfer
Article Text:
Pakistan government statement on Imran Khan's hospital transfer

Poll Vote & Share your view How do you view the involvement of PTI workers during Imran Khan transfer to the hospital? Justified, they were supporting their leader Unsure 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Govt says court order was followed

NEW DELHI: The Pakistan government on Saturday blamed jailed former prime minister Imran Khan ’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party for his transfer to a state-run hospital instead of the private facility ordered by the Supreme Court for his medical checkup.Information minister Attaullah Tarar said the government was forced to take 73-year-old Khan to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) after a large number of PTI workers gathered outside Shifa International Hospital.The development came after Khan’s sister, Uzma Khan, approached the Supreme Court alleging that the government and senior officials had violated its order to shift the former prime minister to the private hospital.The Supreme Court had on August 18 directed authorities to transfer Khan from Adiala jail to Shifa Hospital within two days and keep him there until the next hearing on September 16. Instead, Khan was taken to PIMS and later returned to jail after doctors declared him fit.Tarar alleged that PTI workers gathered along the route to Shifa Hospital, removed barriers and created social media content, leaving authorities with no option but to shift Khan elsewhere.“Contempt has definitely happened,” Tarar said, accusing Khan’s sister and PTI of violating the court’s directions by turning the medical checkup into a political issue.The minister maintained that the government had implemented the Supreme Court’s order “in letter and spirit”. He said the medical examination was conducted transparently, Khan’s sister was present and doctors from Shifa Hospital were involved in the process.The Supreme Court’s order followed months of concerns raised by Khan’s family and supporters over his health, particularly an eye condition diagnosed earlier this year. Khan was taken to PIMS several times after being diagnosed with right central retinal vein occlusion in late January.A report submitted by jail authorities to the Supreme Court said his eye condition had improved significantly and that his vision was “almost normal”.Khan has been lodged in Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail since 2023 in connection with several cases.
Article Summary: Pakistan government blames jailed former prime minister Imran Khan ’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party for his transfer to a state-run hospital. Information minister Attaullah Tarar said the government was forced to take 73-year-old Khan to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences. Tarar alleged that PTI workers gathered along the route to Shifa Hospital, removed barriers and created social media content.

Article Title: Big crisis brewing in Rawalpindi? Pakistan deploys army for ‘sensitive duties’
Article Text:
The decision comes days after a man allegedly linked to former prime minister Imran Khan's party.

Army deployment follows security incident

Rawalpindi has strategic importance

The Pakistan government has authorised the deployment of the army in Rawalpindi for six months following a request from the Punjab home department for what it described as "sensitive security duties".The decision allows three companies of the Pakistan Army to be deployed in the city under Article 245 of the Pakistani Constitution, which permits the armed forces to assist the civil administration in maintaining security."The federal government, exercising the powers conferred under Article 245 of the Constitution of Pakistan, is pleased to authorise the deployment of three companies of the Pakistan Army for sensitive security duties in Rawalpindi," according to a notification issued by the Ministry of Interior and Narcotics Control on Friday.The notification said the deployment was intended to prevent a potential security problem and ensure that authorities could respond quickly if an unexpected situation arose.It said that the decision was taken "to avoid any undesirable situation as well as to respond effectively in any unforeseen situation as per the requirement of the district administration".The decision comes days after a man allegedly linked to former prime minister Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party opened fire at security forces in Rawalpindi.He was subsequently killed in retaliatory firing.State-run PTV News, citing security sources, reported that the attacker was a resident of Khyber district and an "active PTI member". According to the report, a PTI flag, bullets and weapons were recovered from him.The PTI, however, rejected any connection with the incident. The party said it had nothing to do with terrorism and accused authorities of attempting to associate the party with the attack.The deployment is particularly significant because Rawalpindi is home to the Pakistan Army's General Headquarters, the military's top command centre.The city is therefore an important military and administrative centre, and the decision to deploy army personnel there comes amid heightened security concerns following the recent shooting incident.The deployment has been authorised for six months, with the troops to perform duties requested by the district administration under the constitutional provision allowing the military to assist civilian authorities.
Article Summary: Three companies of the Pakistan Army will be deployed in Rawalpindi for six months. The decision comes after a man allegedly linked to Imran Khan's party opened fire in the city. The deployment is intended to prevent a potential security problem and ensure that authorities can respond quickly.

Article Title: 'Repeatedly tortured': Imran Khan's sister alleges abuse in jail as ex-Pakistan PM returns to prison
Article Text:
‘He was repeatedly tortured in jail’: Imran Khan's sister alleges mistreatment

PTI files contempt petition

Supporters gather after brief hospital visit

Pakistan's jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan repeatedly told his sister that he was being tortured in prison, she said on Saturday, a day after he was taken to a state-run hospital for a brief medical examination and sent back to jail.Khan's sister, Uzma Khan, attended his examination at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) in Islamabad and said the former prime minister was physically fit but had repeatedly complained of torture.“Khan told me that he is being repeatedly tortured in prison”, she told the media.The interior and law ministries, along with jail authorities, have not responded to a Reuters request for comment on the allegation.Khan was taken to PIMS overnight on Friday after the Supreme Court had directed authorities to transfer him from Adiala jail to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad for a medical examination. He was declared medically fit and returned to prison within hours.Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party on Saturday filed a contempt petition against the government, accusing authorities of violating the Supreme Court's order by taking him to PIMS instead of the private hospital named by the court.The petition seeks action against senior government officials and asks that Khan be taken to Shifa International Hospital for treatment, PTI legal adviser Naeem Panjutha said."The petition seeks action against the ​prime minister, law minister, information minister" and other government officials, Panjutha said, adding that it also calls for Khan's treatment at the private hospital ordered by the court.The PTI also alleged that Khan was denied access to his personal physician, which it said amounted to another breach of the Supreme Court's directive.A three-judge Supreme Court bench had on Tuesday directed authorities to transfer Khan from Adiala jail to Shifa International Hospital within two days for a medical examination.The PTI interprets the order as requiring Khan to remain under medical supervision until at least mid-September.Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said the decision to take Khan to PIMS instead of the court-named private hospital was made because of security concerns.Khan declared medically fit, sent back to jailKhan was examined by a team of doctors, including an ophthalmologist, cardiologist and physician, before being declared medically fit and sent back to Adiala jail in Rawalpindi."A team of qualified doctors, including an ophthalmologist, a cardiologist and a physician conducted a detailed examination of him and declared him medically fit," Tarar said.Khan has been imprisoned since August 2023 and maintains that the cases against him are politically motivated. The government denies the allegation.His lawyers have previously said his health has deteriorated in prison and that he has suffered substantial loss of vision in his right eye. The government has maintained that medical reports have found no condition requiring immediate treatment.Khan's supporters gathered along roads in Islamabad overnight, throwing flowers at a vehicle believed to be carrying him to the hospital.The scenes were broadcast live on Pakistani television, in a notable departure from recent years when broadcasters often avoided mentioning Khan's name.PTI leaders have warned that the latest developments could increase pressure on the government and fuel fresh demonstrations."After what happened yesterday, the pressure (on authorities) will double," Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi said, adding that preparations for a protest march planned for September 27 had picked up.Khan's arrest and imprisonment have remained a major source of political tension in Pakistan.
